scenarios.title: What Is an IDP?
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks what an Internal Developer Platform actually is, versus 'we have Kubernetes and CI'.
choices: An IDP is the curated set of tools, APIs, and workflows a platform team provides so developers can self-serve infrastructure (environments, deploys, databases) without deep infra expertise — Kubernetes and CI are building blocks, the IDP is the productized layer on top
An IDP is a second Kubernetes cluster reserved for the platform team
An IDP is just a rebranded CI/CD pipeline with a dashboard
An IDP replaces developers; it auto-writes application code
scenarios.why: The distinction is product thinking: raw Kubernetes + CI is a toolkit requiring expertise; an IDP packages them into self-service golden paths with sensible defaults. The platform team treats developers as customers, reducing cognitive load. A cluster alone or a pipeline alone is not a platform.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between handing someone lumber and handing them a furnished room?

scenarios.title: Catalog Before Automation
scenarios.situation: The platform team wants to build a Backstage-style software catalog but can't agree on what goes in it. Half the services have no owner listed anywhere.
scenarios.prompt: What is the minimum viable catalog entry?
choices: For every component: a name, an owner (team or individual), its lifecycle stage, and links to repo/runbook — ownership and findability come before rich metadata; you can enrich later
Full dependency graphs, API specs, and cost data for every service on day one
Only production services; dev and staging services don't need cataloging
The catalog should list infrastructure (clusters, VPCs) instead of software components
scenarios.why: A catalog's core job is answering 'what is this, who owns it, where is it in its lifecycle, where do I find it.' Ownership is the highest-value field — during incidents, 'who owns this' matters more than anything. Starting with the minimal schema gets adoption; demanding complete metadata up front stalls the project.
scenarios.hint: During a 2 AM incident on an unknown service, which single field would you want most?

scenarios.title: Golden Path vs Wild West
scenarios.situation: Teams each built their own deploy pipeline: 14 variants of 'build, test, push, deploy'. The platform team proposes one blessed 'golden path' pipeline. Teams fear losing flexibility.
scenarios.prompt: How should the platform team position the golden path?
choices: Offer the golden path as the default paved road (supported, secure, maintained) while allowing escape hatches for justified exceptions — adoption comes from making the right way the easy way, not from mandates
Mandate the golden path for all teams immediately; uniformity beats autonomy
Abandon the golden path; 14 pipelines is healthy diversity
Make the golden path maximally configurable so it can replicate all 14 variants
scenarios.why: Golden paths work through attraction, not coercion: teams adopt the paved road because it's faster and maintained, and the platform team learns from the escape-hatch cases. Mandates breed shadow IT; infinite configurability recreates the 14 variants inside one template. The paved-road-with-exits model balances standardization and autonomy.
scenarios.hint: Do people use highways because they're forced to, or because they're the fastest maintained route — with exits available?

scenarios.title: Template Sprawl
scenarios.situation: The platform's software templates (scaffolding) have grown to 40 near-identical 'new service' templates. Maintenance is crushing the platform team.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right consolidation move?
choices: Consolidate to a few parameterized templates (language × workload type) with clear versioning and deprecation of the rest — templates are products with a maintenance cost, and 40 variants means 40 things to patch on every CVE
Keep all 40; choice is good for developers
Delete all templates and let teams copy-paste from existing repos
Auto-generate a template per existing service so coverage is complete
scenarios.why: Every template is a maintenance liability: dependency bumps, security patches, and best-practice updates multiply across variants. A small set of parameterized templates (with inputs for the real variations) gives coverage without the combinatorial burden. Deprecation with migration guides moves teams off the long tail.
scenarios.hint: When the next critical CVE hits a base image, how many places will you have to patch?

scenarios.title: Platform API Design
scenarios.situation: The platform team exposes a 'provision database' API. Team A's request returns in 2 seconds; team B's identical request hangs for 20 minutes then fails with no useful error.
scenarios.prompt: What API design principle was violated?
choices: Long-running operations must be asynchronous with status polling (202 + operation ID + status endpoint) and structured, actionable errors — synchronous 20-minute requests hit timeouts everywhere and opaque errors leave callers helpless
Database provisioning should be synchronous; the bug is just a slow backend
The API needs GraphQL; REST cannot express provisioning operations
Errors should return HTTP 200 with an error body so clients don't retry
scenarios.why: Platform APIs wrap operations that take minutes: the correct pattern is accept-and-track (202 Accepted, operation resource, pollable status, webhooks/events on completion). Synchronous designs collapse under proxies, client timeouts, and retries. And errors must be machine-actionable (codes, remediation hints), because the caller is usually automation, not a human reading logs.
scenarios.hint: What happens to an HTTP request that takes 20 minutes, hop by hop? What should the API have returned in second 1?

scenarios.title: Measuring Platform Success
scenarios.situation: The platform team ships features constantly, but engineering leadership asks: 'Is the platform actually helping?' DORA metrics for product teams are flat.
scenarios.prompt: What should the platform team measure?
choices: Developer productivity outcomes: time-to-first-deploy for new services, self-service adoption rate, reduction in infra-related support tickets, and product-team DORA trends for onboarded teams — platform success is measured in developer outcomes, not platform-team output
Number of platform features shipped per quarter; output proves value
Platform team sprint velocity and story points completed
Total lines of Terraform the platform team maintains
scenarios.why: Platforms are force multipliers: their value shows up in the productivity of their users, not their own activity metrics. Time-to-first-commit-to-prod, ticket deflection, and adoption of golden paths directly measure whether the platform reduces friction. Feature counts and velocity measure busyness, and can even be inversely correlated with good platform design (less surface, more leverage).
scenarios.hint: Who is the customer of the platform — and whose numbers should improve if the platform is working?

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Platform Engineering as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Platform Engineering Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Platform Engineering is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Platform Engineering?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Platform Engineering issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Platform Engineering is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Platform Engineering supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Platform Engineering failure in Platform Engineering.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Platform Engineering
evidence: All Platform Engineering components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Start Here: Orientation
domains.summary: How this bootcamp works, how to study platform engineering effectively, the full domain roadmap, and how labs, scenarios, and the mock assessment fit together.

scenarios.title: Desired State, Not Instructions
scenarios.situation: Your teammate debugs a stuck deploy by SSHing into a server and hand-editing a config file. It works — until the next deploy overwrites it.
scenarios.prompt: What principle did they violate, and what is the fix?
choices: They treated the server as mutable and unique instead of declaring the desired state in versioned code. The fix: declare the config in Git, let the platform converge the server to it, and never hand-edit — the next deploy then reproduces the fix instead of destroying it.
They should have edited the file faster so nobody noticed.
Hand-editing is fine; the deploy tool is broken.
They should avoid deploys entirely.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Declarative infrastructure means the code describes the desired end state and the system converges reality to it; imperative hand-edits create drift — reality diverging from code — which the next convergence silently reverts. This is the foundational platform concept: Git as the source of truth, controllers as the enforcers. Every domain in this course (Kubernetes, IaC, GitOps) is an elaboration of it.
scenarios.hint: If the server is rebuilt from code, what happens to the hand-edit?
evidence: Declare desired state in code; the system converges reality to it. Hand-edits are drift.

scenarios.title: The Blast Radius Question
scenarios.situation: You are asked to 'just run this database migration on production.' It is a single command. The requester says it is safe.
scenarios.prompt: What is the platform engineer's first question?
choices: 'Can we do it Friday afternoon?'

'What is the blast radius, and how do we roll back?' — the size of the failure domain and the reversibility of the change determine the process: backups verified, canary or staged rollout, rollback tested before the change, not after.
'How fast can we run it?' — speed is the priority.
No questions needed; the requester said it is safe.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Blast radius and reversibility are the two axes of every operational decision: they determine whether a change gets a maintenance window, a canary, a feature flag, or a rubber stamp. 'The requester said it is safe' is not a control — it is a hope. The platform engineer's job is replacing hope with mechanisms: verified backups, staged rollouts, tested rollbacks.
scenarios.hint: What two facts determine how carefully a change must be handled?
evidence: Failure-domain size + reversibility determine the change process.

scenarios.title: Pets vs Cattle
scenarios.situation: A critical service runs on a single VM lovingly maintained for three years. It fails at 2 AM and nobody can rebuild it — the setup lived in one engineer's head.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what is the platform fix?
choices: Buy a more reliable VM.
Never touch the server again.

The server was a pet — unique, irreplaceable, hand-raised. The fix is cattle: every server built from code (image + config), so any instance can be destroyed and recreated identically. Rebuildability is the property; automation is the mechanism.
The engineer should have documented better — documentation fixes pets.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Pets vs cattle is the mental model for immutable infrastructure: pets get names, nursed back to health, and become single points of failure; cattle get numbers, are replaced not repaired, and are defined entirely by code. Documentation helps but does not fix the category error — only rebuild-from-code does. Kubernetes, image pipelines, and IaC are all cattle-enforcement machinery.
scenarios.hint: If the VM vanished tonight, could you recreate it exactly from code?
evidence: Replace, don't repair. Every server rebuildable from code.

scenarios.title: Planning Your Month
scenarios.situation: You have four weeks. Option 1: watch 40 hours of video about Kubernetes. Option 2: read the lessons, run every lab in a real cluster, keep an incident ledger, and take the mock twice.
scenarios.prompt: Which plan produces an engineer who can pass a technical interview?
choices: Option 1 — coverage is king.
Both are equal; hours are hours.
Option 1, because labs are optional.

Option 2. Interviews probe run knowledge — 'what happens when the probe fails?' — which only comes from breaking things in a terminal. Video builds familiarity; labs build the failure-mode mental models that interviews test. The mock then converts practice into performance under pressure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Technical interviews are adversarial retrieval under pressure: they ask what happens when things break, and only people who have broken things answer well. Forty hours of video produces fluent vocabulary with no underlying model — it collapses at the first 'why.' The ledger-plus-labs loop builds the model; the mock builds the pressure tolerance.
scenarios.hint: Which plan contains failure modes you have personally observed?
evidence: Interview answers come from broken-and-fixed experience, not video.

domains.name: Capstone: Ship a Platform Slice
domains.summary: A guided end-to-end project: ship a working internal developer platform slice — service template, CI pipeline, GitOps delivery, dashboards, and docs — in three phases.

scenarios.title: Template Scope
scenarios.situation: Your capstone template could support Python, Go, Node, and Java from day one. Your mentor says: ship one language first.
choices: Templates should not be tested.

One golden path, proven end to end, teaches you the template mechanics (scaffolding, versioning, testing) with minimum variables. Four languages multiply the failure modes before any path works — you would debug scaffolding AND language quirks simultaneously, learning neither.
Python is the only real language.
Four languages are actually easier.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Platform work is multiplicative complexity: each new dimension (language, cluster, cloud) multiplies the test matrix. The discipline is: prove the machinery on one path, then the second language is a data change, not a new project. This is also how real platform teams sequence — depth before breadth, because a broken golden path poisons adoption.
scenarios.hint: What multiplies when you add a second language before the first works?
evidence: One path proven end to end before expanding; depth before breadth.

scenarios.title: The Skipped Gate
scenarios.situation: Your pipeline's image scan flags a critical CVE. The team is behind schedule and wants to 'ship now, patch later.'
choices: Remove the scan step to avoid future delays.
Ship and hope the CVE is not exploited.

The gate holds: 'ship now, patch later' is how critical CVEs reach production, and the gate exists precisely for schedule pressure — that is when it matters. Offer the fast path instead: the pipeline shows exactly which base image bump clears it, turning days of debate into one PR.
Skip the gate this once; deadlines matter more.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Gates that yield to schedule pressure are theater — their entire purpose is binding when it hurts. The platform move is not just refusal but service: make the compliant path fast (one-click base-image bump, automated rebuild) so 'the right way' is also the easy way. Guardrails that slow developers get bypassed; guardrails that guide get adopted.
scenarios.hint: When is a security gate most valuable: when it is convenient or when it hurts?
evidence: Gates bind hardest under schedule pressure; make compliance the fast path.

scenarios.title: The Untested Rollback
scenarios.situation: Your GitOps setup has never rolled back in production. The team says 'we can always git revert.'
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this confidence?
choices: Nothing — git revert always works.
Rollbacks are never needed with good CI.
Revert is too slow; just roll forward.

An untested rollback is a hope, not a capability: revert mechanics (image availability, migration reversibility, data compatibility) fail in ways only a drill reveals. 'We can always revert' must be proven in staging regularly, or the first real incident becomes the first test.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Rollback has failure modes: the old image may be garbage-collected, database migrations may not reverse, the revert may conflict with newer commits. A rollback drill in staging exposes these cheaply; a production incident exposes them expensively. Platform maturity is measured in proven recoveries, not in deployment frequency alone.
scenarios.hint: What could make 'git revert' fail at 3 AM?
evidence: Untested rollback is hope; drill it in staging or debug it in prod.

scenarios.title: Docs as UI
scenarios.situation: Your platform works, but new teams take two weeks to onboard. The docs are a wiki page saying 'ask in #platform-help.'
choices: The platform's human interface is missing: docs are part of the product — quickstart, architecture, runbooks for the top failure modes. Every 'ask in chat' is a support ticket the docs should have answered; onboarding time is the platform's latency metric.
New teams are slow learners.
Wikis are the problem; buy a docs tool.
Onboarding time does not matter.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A platform is a product whose UI is docs, CLIs, and error messages. 'Ask in chat' scales with team size — linearly and painfully — while docs scale sublinearly. The fix is specific: a 5-minute quickstart (time-boxed proof), runbooks for the failures you have actually seen, and ownership/escalation paths. Measure time-to-first-deploy; watch it drop as docs improve.
scenarios.hint: What scales better with team count: chat answers or written runbooks?
evidence: Docs, CLIs, error messages are the platform's human interface; measure onboarding time.

scenarios.title: Vanity vs Signal
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks for platform metrics. Candidate set A: number of services onboarded, clusters managed, pipelines run. Candidate set B: lead time for changes, failed-deployment rate, time-to-first-deploy, toil hours.
choices: Neither; platforms cannot be measured.

Set B. Set A measures platform activity (vanity) — it grows with adoption regardless of value. Set B measures outcomes developers feel: speed, reliability, and toil. A platform with 200 onboarded services and 3-week lead times is failing; the metrics should say so.
Set A — bigger numbers impress leadership.
Both equally; metrics are metrics.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Goodhart's law applies: teams optimize what is measured, so measure outcomes not activity. DORA-style metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate, recovery time) plus toil and onboarding time tell you whether the platform helps. 'Services onboarded' incentivizes forced migration; 'lead time' incentivizes actual enablement. Choose metrics you would want applied to you.
scenarios.hint: Which set would catch a platform that onboards everyone but helps no one?
evidence: Measure outcomes (lead time, reliability, toil), not activity (counts).

domains.name: Kubernetes Platform
domains.summary: Running Kubernetes as a platform: cluster architecture, workloads, networking, operators, and multi-cluster operations.

scenarios.title: The CrashLoop Mystery
scenarios.situation: A pod CrashLoops after a deploy. Logs show the app starts, then the pod is killed and restarted. The app runs fine locally.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: Kubernetes is broken.
The image is corrupted.

A misconfigured liveness probe: the probe fails (wrong path, too-aggressive timing), so Kubernetes kills a healthy container. The app is fine; the platform's health check is wrong. Check probe config first — it is the classic 'the monitor is the murderer' case.
The app is broken in production.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. CrashLoopBackOff with a locally-fine app screams liveness probe: the kubelet kills containers whose liveness probe fails, and a probe hitting the wrong port/path or with initialDelaySeconds shorter than startup time murders healthy apps on a loop. Diagnose with kubectl describe pod (probe failure events) and fix the probe — or the startup time. Readiness failures, by contrast, remove from service without restarts: probe type determines the failure mode.
scenarios.hint: Does a failed liveness probe restart, while a failed readiness probe only removes from service?
evidence: Liveness failure = restart. Readiness failure = removed from endpoints.

scenarios.title: The :latest Incident
scenarios.situation: Production runs image: api:latest. A deploy 'changes nothing' but behavior changes — someone pushed to :latest. Rollback is impossible: nobody knows which digest was running.
choices: Stop pushing to :latest.
Ban deploys.
Use bigger version numbers.

Pin immutable digests or semantic tags in production manifests: image: api:1.4.2 (or the sha256 digest). :latest is mutable — it names whatever was pushed last, making deploys unreproducible and rollbacks guesswork. The tag is part of the desired state; mutable tags are undesired states.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. :latest is not a version — it is a mutable pointer, so 'what is running' becomes unknowable and 'roll back' becomes meaningless. Immutable tags (or digests) make the manifest a complete, reproducible declaration: the same manifest always yields the same containers. This is declarative infrastructure applied to images — and the GitOps repo should record the exact tag per environment.
scenarios.hint: Can you reproduce yesterday's production from the manifest alone?
evidence: Never :latest in prod. Pin tags/digests; manifests must be reproducible.

scenarios.title: The Database in a Deployment
scenarios.situation: A team runs PostgreSQL as a Deployment with a single replica and an emptyDir volume. The pod reschedules to another node; all data is gone.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong at the design level?
choices: Two errors: a Deployment (wrong controller — no stable identity) and emptyDir (ephemeral storage tied to the pod's life). Databases need StatefulSet (stable name, ordered) plus PersistentVolumeClaims (storage that outlives the pod). The design treated state as disposable; state disagreed.
Kubernetes deleted the data maliciously.
PostgreSQL is unsuitable for Kubernetes.
emptyDir is broken.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. emptyDir lives and dies with the pod — it is scratch space, not storage. Persistent data needs a PersistentVolume (the storage) claimed by the pod (the PVC), surviving rescheduling. And StatefulSets exist precisely because databases care which pod they are: stable network identity and stable storage identity. The rule: match the controller to the statefulness — stateless → Deployment, identity+storage → StatefulSet.
scenarios.hint: What survives a pod reschedule: emptyDir or a PersistentVolumeClaim?
evidence: StatefulSet + PVC. emptyDir is scratch; Deployments have no stable identity.

scenarios.title: The Lateral Movement
scenarios.situation: An attacker compromises one pod and immediately reaches the database pod, the cache, and the internal API — no policy stopped them.
choices: More CPU for the pods.
The attacker was too skilled; nothing helps.

NetworkPolicy: with no policies, the cluster network is flat — every pod can reach every pod. Default-deny ingress plus explicit allow rules per workload would have contained the breach to the compromised pod. Network segmentation is the containment layer.
A stronger firewall at the cluster edge.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B (index 1). Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is the pod-level firewall: without any policy, all pod-to-pod traffic is allowed — the default is open, not closed. The fix is default-deny plus explicit allows, which turns the network into documented, intended paths. Edge firewalls do not help: the attack moved laterally inside the cluster, where the edge never sees it. Defense in depth starts at the workload.
scenarios.hint: Where did the attacker move: through the edge firewall or inside the flat pod network?
evidence: Default-deny + explicit allow. Flat pod networks enable lateral movement.

scenarios.title: The Brain Injury
scenarios.situation: The etcd cluster loses quorum during a storage incident. Workloads keep running, but kubectl hangs and no deploys work.
scenarios.prompt: Why do workloads survive while control fails, and what is the priority?
choices: The cluster is dead; rebuild everything.
Wait — etcd heals itself.

Workloads survive because kubelets run from cached state — they do not need the API server moment to moment. But nothing can change: no scheduling, no scaling, no deploys. Priority: restore etcd quorum from backup or surviving members — the control plane is the patient, workloads are stable.
Restart all workloads immediately.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. This is the control-plane/data-plane split: the data plane (running pods) is designed to survive control-plane outages, but the system is frozen — it cannot adapt to new failures. etcd quorum loss is the most serious cluster incident: restore from snapshot to a healthy member set, verify, then unfreeze. Prevention: 3+ members across zones, dedicated fast disks, monitored, and backups tested by restore — not by existence.
scenarios.hint: Which plane runs the pods, and which plane changes them?
evidence: Data plane survives; control plane frozen. Restore quorum from backup.

scenarios.title: The Noisy Neighbor
scenarios.situation: One team's batch job consumes all node CPU; latency-sensitive APIs on the same nodes degrade. No limits are set anywhere.
choices: Buy bigger nodes.
Ban batch jobs.
Move the APIs to dedicated nodes (and repeat for every workload).

Resource requests and limits on every workload: requests for scheduling (guaranteed share), limits for enforcement (ceiling). Plus LimitRanges for defaults and ResourceQuotas per namespace so no team can starve others. The platform sets the defaults; teams tune within them.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Without requests/limits, the scheduler cannot place workloads intelligently and the kernel cannot arbitrate contention — it is tragedy of the commons with extra steps. Requests = scheduling guarantee (and QoS class input); limits = hard ceiling. LimitRange supplies defaults so teams cannot forget; ResourceQuota caps namespaces. Dedicated nodes per workload is the pets-vs-cattle regression — solve it with the scheduler, not with hardware.
scenarios.hint: Who arbitrates CPU contention when nothing is set?
evidence: Requests schedule, limits enforce. Defaults via LimitRange, caps via Quota.

scenarios.title: The Bad Rollout
scenarios.situation: A new version rolls out; error rates climb. The deploy used RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0, and readiness probes are configured.
scenarios.prompt: Why didn't the rollout stop itself, and what is the recovery?
choices: maxUnavailable: 0 prevents all rollouts.
Readiness probes stop rollouts automatically.

RollingUpdate does not auto-rollback on error metrics — it only respects probe failures and maxUnavailable during the rollout mechanics. Recovery: kubectl rollout undo (revision history) or a GitOps revert, then investigate with the preserved failed revision. For automatic halting, add progressive delivery (canary analysis on metrics).
Kubernetes should have known; file a bug.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A (index 0). Kubernetes rollouts are mechanical, not intelligent: they proceed unless probes fail or the rollout itself errors. Error-rate awareness requires progressive delivery tooling (Argo Rollouts, Flagger) that analyzes metrics and halts/promotes automatically. The immediate recovery is the revision system — rollout undo — which is why keeping revision history matters. Lesson: basic rollouts need human or canary supervision; 'deploy and hope' is not a strategy.
scenarios.hint: Does a standard RollingUpdate watch your error metrics?
evidence: RollingUpdate is mechanical; use revisions to undo, canary analysis to auto-halt.

domains.name: CI/CD Pipelines
domains.summary: From commit to production: pipeline anatomy, artifacts, testing gates, progressive delivery, and pipeline security.

scenarios.title: The Red-Normal Pipeline
scenarios.situation: The e2e suite flakes 30% of the time. Developers now re-run failed pipelines reflexively and merge on green re-runs. Last week a real regression shipped because 'it always goes green on retry.'
choices: Tell developers to retry more carefully.
Delete the e2e suite entirely.
Make the suite blocking-but-retryable forever.

Quarantine the flaky tests immediately: move them to a non-blocking suite with an owner and a fix deadline, and keep the blocking line fast and reliable. A gate that cries wolf trains developers to ignore gates — reliability of the signal matters more than coverage of the suite.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Flaky gates destroy the pipeline's epistemic value: once developers learn red is meaningless, real red ships. The discipline is quarantine (flakes run informationally, owned, with a deadline) plus root-causing (timing, shared state, external deps). Coverage lost temporarily is cheaper than a team that ignores CI. The metric to watch: re-run rate — it should be near zero.
scenarios.hint: What did the team learn from 30% flakiness: to fix tests, or to ignore red?
evidence: Quarantine flakes; blocking gates must be fast AND reliable.

scenarios.title: Works on Stage
scenarios.situation: A release passes all tests on staging but fails in production. Investigation: staging and prod were built from the same commit — but at different times, with different base images.
choices: Build once, promote everywhere: rebuilding per environment reintroduces variance (base images, dependencies, timestamps) that invalidates everything staging proved. The artifact must be built once and promoted by digest through every environment.
Staging is useless; test in prod.
The tests were wrong.
Commits should be frozen.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Staging's entire value is proving the artifact that ships; rebuilding for prod tests a different artifact and voids the proof. Immutable artifacts promoted by digest make 'works on stage' meaningful — the bits are identical. This is why pipelines separate build (once) from promote (many): the promotion is a reference change, not a rebuild.
scenarios.hint: Were staging and production running the same bits?
evidence: One immutable artifact promoted by digest; never rebuild per environment.

scenarios.title: The Silent Rollout Failure
scenarios.situation: A canary deploys to 5% of traffic. Error rates triple on the canary — but the rollout continues to 100% because 'the canary looked fine on the dashboard.'
choices: Dashboards are useless.

The analysis: a canary without automated metric comparison is just a slow big-bang. Progressive delivery requires the rollout to watch error/latency metrics and halt or roll back automatically — human dashboard-glancing does not scale and does not trigger at 3 AM.
Canary deployments do not work.
5% was too small to matter.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The canary pattern's value is the judgment loop: compare canary vs baseline on defined metrics, promote or halt automatically. Without analysis, you get the worst of both — slow rollout AND full blast radius. Tools like Argo Rollouts/Flagger encode this; the alternative is a human watching graphs, which fails exactly when it matters (off-hours, subtle regressions).
scenarios.hint: Who was watching the canary's metrics at 3 AM?
evidence: Automated metric comparison with auto-halt; dashboards don't page.

scenarios.title: The Leaked CI Key
scenarios.situation: A long-lived AWS key stored in CI secrets appears in a public build log. It had full admin access and was two years old.
scenarios.prompt: What are the two fixes (immediate and structural)?
choices: Make the key longer.
Restrict who can view logs.

Immediate: revoke the key, audit CloudTrail for misuse, rotate anything it touched. Structural: replace long-lived keys with OIDC federation (short-lived, no stored secret) and scope pipeline roles to least privilege — so the next leak is a 1-hour token, not a 2-year admin key.
Delete the build log and hope.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Incident response (revoke, audit, rotate) handles this leak; architecture (OIDC, least privilege, short-lived) prevents the class. Long-lived admin keys in CI are the worst combination: maximum blast radius, maximum lifetime, in the system most likely to leak them (logs are exfiltrated constantly). The structural fix removes the secret category entirely.
scenarios.hint: How long should a CI credential live, and how much should it access?
evidence: OIDC + short-lived + least privilege. Revoke, audit, rotate on leak.

scenarios.title: The Irreversible Migration
scenarios.situation: A deploy includes a migration that drops a column. The deploy fails halfway; rollback is impossible — the old code needs the dropped column.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct migration discipline?
choices: Never migrate databases.
Test migrations harder.
Drop columns on Fridays when nobody is watching.

Expand-then-contract: additive changes first (add column, dual-write), migrate data, switch readers, then remove the old — every step independently deployable and reversible. Destructive changes never ride with code deploys; they follow after the code no longer needs the old shape.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The expand-contract pattern makes each deploy safe in both directions: at every point, old and new code both work. The failing pattern — destructive migration bundled with the code change — couples the deploy to a point of no return. Migrations are the hardest part of progressive delivery precisely because data cannot be 'rolled back' like stateless code; the discipline compensates.
scenarios.hint: At which step could you still roll back safely?
evidence: Additive first, migrate, switch, remove. Never bundle destructive changes.

scenarios.title: The 45-Minute Pipeline
scenarios.situation: The pipeline takes 45 minutes. Developers batch huge PRs to 'make it worth the wait,' and each batch is riskier than the last.
scenarios.prompt: What is the dynamic, and the fix?
choices: Bigger batches are fine with good tests.

Slow feedback inverts CI: developers batch to amortize the wait, batches raise risk, risk raises failure rates, failures raise caution — a doom loop. Fix: parallelize test shards, cache aggressively, split suites (fast blocking, slow nightly), and budget the inner loop under 10 minutes.
Developers should be more patient.
Run the pipeline less often.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A (index 0). Pipeline speed is a behavioral lever, not just convenience: the commit-to-signal time determines batch size, and batch size determines risk. Every minute of pipeline latency is paid in larger, scarier changes. The fixes are mechanical (sharding, caching, suite splitting) but the goal is behavioral: make small commits the path of least resistance.
scenarios.hint: Does the 45-minute wait produce smaller or larger changes?
evidence: Slow pipelines cause batching; batching causes risk. Budget <10 min.

scenarios.title: The Malicious PR
scenarios.situation: A contributor's PR edits the pipeline definition to exfiltrate secrets. It needs a maintainer's approval to merge — but the pipeline RUNS on the PR to 'test the changes.'
choices: Pipelines should not run on PRs.

Running untrusted pipeline code with trusted credentials: PR builds from forks must run with minimal permissions (no secrets, read-only) — the dangerous pattern is executing a stranger's YAML with your deploy keys. Separate 'test the code' (untrusted, sandboxed) from 'test the pipeline change' (trusted review required).
Open source is insecure.
Maintainers should review faster.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. CI systems that execute PR pipeline definitions with production secrets hand attackers a credential-exfiltration primitive: submit YAML that prints secrets to logs. The fix is privilege separation — fork PRs get no secrets and restricted tokens (pull_request vs pull_request_target semantics), and pipeline-definition changes require maintainer approval before the new definition executes. This is the pwn-request pattern; every major CI has been bitten.
scenarios.hint: Whose code ran with whose credentials?
evidence: Fork PRs get no secrets; pipeline changes need approval before execution.

domains.name: Infrastructure as Code
domains.summary: Terraform and beyond: declarative infrastructure, state management, modules, drift detection, and policy as code.

scenarios.title: The Skipped Plan
scenarios.situation: An engineer runs terraform apply directly on production 'because the change is small.' The apply replaces the database — the plan would have shown -/+ (destroy and recreate).
scenarios.prompt: What is the rule, and why?
choices: Never apply without reviewing the plan in production: the plan is the change's preview, and -/+ (replacement) vs ~ (in-place update) is the difference between a tweak and an outage. 'Small change' is a feeling; the plan is a fact. The rule is mechanical so it works when judgment is tired.
Small changes do not need review.
Terraform should refuse replacements.
Databases should not be in Terraform.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The plan/apply split exists because infrastructure changes are hard to preview and easy to regret: replacement (-/+) destroys before creating, and for stateful resources that means data loss. Making plan-review mandatory (CI plan on PR, apply only the reviewed plan file) turns discipline into process. The engineer's error was not ignorance but process bypass — which is why the fix is a gate, not a lecture.
scenarios.hint: What symbol would have warned them, and what does it mean?
evidence: Review +/~/-; -/+ means destroy-and-recreate. Never skip in prod.

scenarios.title: The Corrupted State
scenarios.situation: Two engineers apply simultaneously from local state files. The applies interleave; state now claims resources that do not exist and misses ones that do.
scenarios.prompt: What broke, and what is the structural fix?
choices: Delete the state and re-import everything weekly.

Concurrent uncoordinated writes to unprotected state: without remote state with locking, two writers corrupt the shared memory. Fix: remote backend (S3+DynamoDB/Terraform Cloud) with mandatory locking, one writer at a time (CI-serialized applies), and state versioning for recovery.
Terraform is unreliable; use the console.
The engineers should coordinate better verbally.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. State is a shared mutable data structure — it needs the same protections as any other: a single store, atomic locked writes, and serialized access. Local state files make every apply a race. The CI-serialized pattern (applies only from the pipeline, one at a time) removes the human race entirely. Verbal coordination is not a concurrency control.
scenarios.hint: What concurrency primitive was missing?
evidence: State is shared mutable data: one store, locked writes, serialized applies.

scenarios.title: The Console Edit
scenarios.situation: Someone opens a security group to 0.0.0.0/0 in the console 'temporarily' for debugging. Six months later it is still open, and nobody remembers why.
choices: Audit annually.
Console edits are fine; Terraform will catch up.

Make drift visible and temporary impossible: nightly plan-only drift detection alerting on diffs, IAM policies denying console edits on managed resources (or alerting on them), and a culture rule — the console is read-only for IaC-managed infrastructure. 'Temporary' console changes are permanent until proven otherwise.
Trust engineers to remember.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Drift is entropy: every manual change is a future incident or audit finding, and human memory is not a change-management system. The layered defense — detect (nightly plans), prevent (IAM deny), cultural (console read-only) — treats the console as the exception path, not a workflow. The security group left open is the canonical example because it is both common and breach-shaped.
scenarios.hint: How would you know about the open rule tonight, without asking anyone?

scenarios.title: The Mega-Module
scenarios.situation: A 'platform' module takes 47 variables, provisions VPC+DB+K8s+monitoring, and nobody dares change it. Teams copy-paste it and override variables they barely understand.
choices: 47 variables is fine; document them.
Modules are a mistake; inline everything.
Teams should read more carefully.

Wrong abstraction granularity: the mega-module couples unrelated lifecycles and forces every consumer to understand everything. Fix: small focused modules (network, database) composed in root modules per environment — composition over configuration, extracted at the third copy not the first.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. A module with 47 variables is not reusable — it is a framework with a learning curve, and consumers copy-paste instead of understanding. Small modules with narrow contracts compose: the VPC module does networking, the DB module does databases, the root module wires them. The 'third copy' rule prevents premature abstraction in the other direction. Reusability is measured by confident use, not by variable count.
scenarios.hint: Do consumers understand the module, or copy-paste it in fear?
evidence: Small focused modules, composed. Extract at third copy.

scenarios.title: The Audit Surprise
scenarios.situation: An auditor finds 30 unencrypted databases and 12 public storage buckets. Each was 'a quick test that became production.'
scenarios.prompt: What would have prevented this class of findings?
choices: Trust engineers to remember encryption.

Policy as code evaluated on every plan: deny rules for unencrypted storage and public exposure, blocking the PR before the resource exists. Prevention at plan time beats detection at audit time — the auditor should find nothing because the pipeline never allowed it.
More auditors, more often.
A wiki page about encryption.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A (index 0). The failure mode is 'quick test becomes production' — human memory and wiki pages do not survive it, but a plan-time gate does: the unencrypted database simply cannot be created through the pipeline. Five deny rules (encryption, public exposure, tagging, wildcard IAM, open ingress) prevent the misconfigurations behind most breach headlines. The auditor's job becomes verifying the gates, not counting violations.
scenarios.hint: At what point is the cheapest place to catch an unencrypted database?
evidence: Deny misconfigurations in CI on the plan; auditors verify gates.

scenarios.title: The Orphaned Resources
scenarios.situation: A team deletes their Terraform state file to 'start fresh.' The resources still exist in the cloud — and still bill — but Terraform no longer knows about them.
scenarios.prompt: What happened, and what is the recovery?
choices: Start fresh is correct; orphans are fine.

They deleted the map, not the territory: state tracks real resources; deleting it orphans them (still real, still billing, now unmanaged). Recovery: terraform import each resource back into state, or delete them via the console/CLI and re-create properly. Prevention: remote versioned state — you cannot 'lose' what is backed up.
The resources are gone; nothing to do.
Terraform deleted them automatically.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. State is the mapping between declarations and reality — destroying the mapping does not destroy the resources, it just blinds Terraform to them. This is why state lives in a versioned remote backend: accidental deletion is recoverable, and 'start fresh' happens via targeted state surgery (mv/rm with intent), not file deletion. Orphaned resources are a billing and security liability — they exist outside all policy.
scenarios.hint: Did deleting the state file delete the cloud resources?
evidence: Deleting state orphans resources. Import to recover; version state.

scenarios.title: The Replacement Surprise
scenarios.situation: A plan shows aws_db_instance.main must be replaced (-/+) because someone changed an immutable attribute (engine version via the wrong argument). The engineer applies anyway 'to get it over with.'
scenarios.prompt: Why is this the most dangerous common Terraform mistake?
choices: Terraform would refuse.
The -/+ symbol means in-place update.

Replacement means destroy-then-create: for stateful resources, the data is destroyed with the old instance before the new one exists. -/+ on a database without a snapshot strategy is data loss by automation — the plan announced it, and the engineer confirmed it.
Replacements are always safe.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The -/+ symbol is Terraform's loudest warning: this resource will be destroyed and recreated. For stateless resources it is routine; for stateful ones it is potentially catastrophic. The discipline: read every -/+ as 'what dies here?', snapshot before stateful replacements, and use lifecycle prevent_destroy on resources that must never be casually replaced. The plan told the truth — the failure was not reading it.
scenarios.hint: What does -/+ do to the old resource before creating the new one?
evidence: Destroy-then-create. Read every -/+ as 'what dies here?'

domains.name: Observability & SRE
domains.summary: Seeing inside systems: metrics, logs, traces, SLOs, alerting discipline, and incident response.

scenarios.title: The Midnight Page
scenarios.situation: You are paged at midnight: error budget burn rate is 14x. The dashboard shows errors started 20 minutes ago, right after a deploy.
choices: Page three more people to brainstorm.

Check the deploy as the rollback candidate: the temporal correlation (errors start at deploy time) plus the burn rate makes rollback the highest-expected-value mitigation. Mitigate first via the runbook's first step; root-cause after service is restored.
SSH into production and start debugging the code.
Wait to see if it resolves itself.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Incident discipline: mitigate before root-causing, and the most recent deploy is the prime suspect by base rates (most incidents are caused by changes). The runbook's first action exists so the on-call does not improvise at midnight. Debugging code during the fire extends user impact; rollback is reversible and fast. Root cause gets its full investigation after mitigation — the postmortem, not the incident, is the classroom.
scenarios.hint: What restores service fastest: debugging or rolling back the correlated change?
evidence: Page on budget burn; mitigate (rollback) first, root-cause later.

scenarios.title: The Wrong SLI
scenarios.situation: Team A alerts on 'CPU > 80%.' Team B alerts on 'p99 latency > 500ms and error rate > 0.1%.' Both get paged regularly; only Team B's pages correlate with user complaints.
choices: Team B is lucky.
Alert on everything to be safe.

SLIs must measure what users feel: latency and errors are user-facing; CPU is a cause, not a symptom. Paging on causes pages during harmless spikes and misses real degradation at low CPU. Alert on symptoms (or budget burn); investigate causes after.
CPU alerting is more precise.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The symptom/cause distinction is the core of alerting discipline: symptoms (user-facing: errors, latency) determine paging; causes (CPU, disk, queue depth) determine tickets and dashboards. Paging on causes produces alert fatigue (pages during benign spikes) and missed incidents (user pain without CPU pain). Team B's pages correlate with complaints because they measure the complaint.
scenarios.hint: Do users feel your CPU?
evidence: Alert on symptoms users feel; causes get tickets, not pages.

scenarios.title: The Empty Budget
scenarios.situation: The error budget is exhausted with two weeks left in the month. Product wants to ship a risky feature 'because the quarter ends.'
scenarios.prompt: What does the error-budget policy say?
choices: The budget is the contract: exhausted budget means feature freeze and reliability work until budget recovers. The policy exists precisely for quarter-end pressure — that is when it matters. Offer the trade explicitly: buy back budget (reliability work) or wait.
Ship it; quarters matter more than budgets.
The budget is advisory.
Lower the SLO to create budget.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D (index 3). Error budgets convert reliability debates into arithmetic: the policy was agreed when everyone was calm, so it binds when everyone is stressed. Exhausted budget → freeze is the mechanism that protects users from quarter-end risk-taking. Lowering the SLO to manufacture budget is accounting fraud — it changes the promise to users, which requires renegotiation, not arithmetic.
scenarios.hint: When is the budget policy most valuable: when convenient or when pressured?
evidence: Exhausted budget = feature freeze. The policy binds under pressure.

scenarios.title: The Debugging Commander
scenarios.situation: During a major incident, the incident commander starts debugging a hunch personally and stops coordinating. Updates stop; two responders duplicate each other's work.
choices: Role discipline: the commander's job is coordination, timeline, and decisions — not debugging. A debugging commander abandons the role, and the incident loses its coordinator: duplicated work, lost timeline, silent stakeholders. The fix is structural: commanders command, responders respond.
The commander should debug faster.
More responders would help.
The hunch was probably right.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Incident roles exist because incidents fail on coordination before technology: without a commander, nobody prioritizes, the timeline dies, and stakeholders escalate blindly. The temptation is real (the commander is often the best debugger) — which is why the rule is absolute. If the commander must debug, they hand off command first. Two roles, one person, zero coordination is the failure mode.
scenarios.hint: Who was coordinating while the commander debugged?
evidence: Commanders coordinate; they don't debug. Hand off before diving in.

scenarios.title: The Human Error
scenarios.situation: A postmortem concludes: 'Root cause: engineer ran the wrong command.' The action item: 'Be more careful.'
choices: Postmortems are bureaucratic anyway.

It stops at the human instead of the system: 'why was the destructive command available without a guardrail? why did the tooling allow it? why no confirmation?' — 'be more careful' is not an action item (no system change, no owner-able work). Blameless postmortems fix systems; blameful ones fix nothing and teach hiding mistakes.
It correctly identified the cause.
'Be more careful' is actionable.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. 'Human error' is not a root cause — it is the starting point of the analysis. The five-whys must continue past the person to the system: the missing guardrail, the ambiguous command, the absent confirmation. And 'be more careful' fails every action-item test (specific? owned? dated? verifiable?). Worse, blame teaches the org to hide mistakes — destroying the reporting culture that reliability depends on.
scenarios.hint: What system allowed the wrong command to work?
evidence: Humans aren't root causes. Fix systems; action items need owners+dates.

scenarios.title: The Slow Checkout
scenarios.situation: Checkout p99 latency tripled. Metrics show the frontend is slow; logs show nothing unusual; the database looks healthy.
scenarios.prompt: What is the next diagnostic step?
choices: Restart the database.
Increase all timeouts.

Trace a slow checkout request end to end: the trace's span waterfall shows which service call consumes the time — metrics localized the symptom to the frontend, but only the trace reveals the downstream dependency (payments? inventory? fraud check?) actually responsible. Metric → trace → log is the investigation order.
Add more frontend servers.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The three pillars have an investigation order: metrics detect and localize (frontend slow), traces attribute across services (which downstream span eats the time), logs explain the instance (what the slow service was doing). Skipping to fixes (more servers, restarts) treats the symptom's location as its cause — the classic distributed-systems error. The trace is the only tool that sees across service boundaries.
scenarios.hint: Which tool sees across service boundaries?
evidence: Metrics detect, traces attribute, logs explain. Follow the order.

scenarios.title: The Ignored Page
scenarios.situation: An on-call engineer sleeps through a page — the fifth that night, the previous four false alarms. The real incident burns for two hours.
choices: The engineer is at fault; escalate discipline.
Buy louder pagers.
Five pages is normal; try harder.

Alert fatigue treated as a personal failing: four false alarms trained the human to ignore the fifth. The fix is alert hygiene — every alert must earn its page (burn-rate or user symptom), with tune/silence/delete for the rest. The engineer's sleep was the predictable output of a noisy system.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Alert fatigue is a reliability incident with a human symptom: noisy alerting degrades the response system (the human) until real pages are missed. Blaming the engineer repeats the postmortem error — the system produced the behavior. The metric is pages per on-call shift; the discipline is that every page must require human action now. Four false alarms were four unaddressed bugs in the alerting system.
scenarios.hint: What trained the engineer to ignore the fifth page?
evidence: Noisy pages train humans to ignore real ones. Tune, silence, or delete.

domains.name: Developer Experience
domains.summary: The platform as a product: golden paths, self-service, documentation, and measuring what developers feel.

scenarios.title: The Two-Week Onboarding
scenarios.situation: New developers take two weeks to ship their first change: three ticket queues, a wiki scavenger hunt, and tribal knowledge from whoever is online.
scenarios.prompt: What is the platform diagnosis and prescription?
choices: More wiki pages.
Assign each hire a buddy and call it done.

The golden path's first hour is broken: prescribe a scaffold-to-prod quickstart under 15 minutes, self-service provisioning replacing the ticket queues, and failure-shaped docs replacing the wiki hunt. Measure time-to-first-deploy; treat every week over target as a platform bug.
New hires are slow; accept it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Onboarding time is the platform's latency metric — it measures the golden path's actual usability. Ticket queues are the symptom of missing self-service; wiki hunts of missing doc shapes; tribal knowledge of missing runbooks. Buddies help but do not scale; the platform must make the first hour self-serve. Time it with real new hires, not with the team that built it.
scenarios.hint: What does two-week onboarding measure about the platform?
evidence: Time-to-first-deploy measures the golden path; fix the first hour.

scenarios.title: The Shadow Platform
scenarios.situation: Three teams built their own deploy scripts, bypassing the platform. The platform team calls it non-compliance; the teams call it survival.
choices: The platform team: mandate compliance immediately.
Both: let a thousand platforms bloom.
Nobody: ignore it.

The teams: shadow platforms are user research — they reveal where the golden path fails (too slow, too rigid, missing features). The platform response is product work: interview the bypassers, fix the gaps, make the path better than the workaround. Mandates without fixes breed more shadows.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Every shadow platform is a vote of no confidence with a feature request attached: the bypassers did product discovery for you. Mandating compliance without fixing the underlying gaps just drives the shadow deeper underground. The mature response treats bypassers as the most valuable user segment — they cared enough to build an alternative — and wins them back with a better path.
scenarios.hint: What feature request is the shadow platform making?
evidence: Bypass = user research. Interview bypassers; fix the path.

scenarios.title: The Mandate Backfire
scenarios.situation: Leadership mandates: 'all teams on the platform by Q3.' Teams comply nominally — wrapping old scripts in platform-shaped shells — while real work bypasses it.
choices: Adoption cannot be mandated into existence: nominal compliance without belief produces cargo-cult usage that costs more than the old way. Adoption follows value — the path must be better, not just required. Mandates skip the product work (fixing gaps, proving value) that earns real adoption.
The deadline was too generous.
Teams are resistant to change generally.
The mandate needed stricter enforcement.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Mandated adoption measures compliance theater: teams optimize for the appearance of usage while routing around the pain. Real adoption is a product outcome — it happens when the golden path is genuinely the easiest way. The mandate's proper form is a goal ('80% of deploys via golden path by Q3') paired with resourcing the product work to earn it, not a decree.
scenarios.hint: Did the mandate produce adoption or the appearance of adoption?
evidence: Compliance theater. Earn adoption with a better path, not decrees.

scenarios.title: The Wiki Nobody Reads
scenarios.situation: The platform wiki has 200 pages. Developers ask in chat instead. The docs team proposes 200 more pages.
choices: 200 pages is not enough.
Chat should be banned to force doc usage.

Wrong doc shapes: developers need task-shaped how-tos, failure-shaped runbooks, and a 15-minute quickstart — not 200 reference pages. Chat-asking is the signal: the needed shape does not exist. More pages of the wrong shape deepens the hole; the fix is four shapes, tested with real users.
Developers are lazy readers.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B (index 1). Documentation failure is a product failure: the docs do not match the jobs developers hire them for (ship fast, fix failures). Reference pages answer 'what exists?'; developers ask 'how do I...?' and 'it broke, now what?' — different shapes. The chat channel is free user research: every repeated question names a missing doc. Banning chat treats the symptom; shipping the right shapes treats the cause.
scenarios.hint: What question shapes do developers actually ask?
evidence: Quickstart, how-to, reference, runbook. Match the job, not the wiki.

scenarios.title: The Survey Nobody Acts On
scenarios.situation: The quarterly dev survey shows 'shipping is painful: 2.1/5' with 40 comments naming the flaky pipeline. Nothing changes for three quarters.
choices: Developers complain too much.
2.1/5 is fine.

The feedback loop: surveys without visible action teach developers that feedback is theater, and response rates collapse. Every survey needs a published response ('you said X, we shipped Y') within the quarter. Unactioned research is worse than no research — it spends trust.
The survey questions were wrong.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. User research is a loop — collect, act, report — and breaking any link breaks trust in the whole. The 40 comments naming the pipeline were a free roadmap; ignoring them for three quarters taught the org that the platform team does not listen. The fix is cadence discipline: small survey, fast visible action on the top theme, public 'you said / we did.' Trust compounds; so does distrust.
scenarios.hint: What did three quarters of inaction teach the developers?
evidence: Survey -> act -> report, visibly, quarterly. Unactioned research spends trust.

scenarios.title: The Ten-Minute Test Loop
scenarios.situation: Developers stopped running tests locally: the suite takes 10 minutes. They push and 'let CI find out.' CI is now the test runner, and it is drowning.
choices: Ban pushing without local tests.
Buy bigger CI runners.
Tests are optional anyway.

Fix the inner loop: split the suite (fast unit subset in seconds, full suite in CI), parallelize, and make the local loop sub-minute. Developers optimize for loop speed rationally — a 10-minute local loop guarantees CI-as-tester. The platform owns the local story, not just the cluster.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Behavior follows loop speed: developers will always choose the fastest feedback path, so the platform must make the right path the fast path. Mandating local tests without fixing the 10-minute loop is mandating pain — compliance will be nominal. Split, parallelize, cache: the local subset should run in seconds. CI keeps the full suite; the laptop keeps the fast one.
scenarios.hint: Why did developers rationally choose CI as their test runner?
evidence: Developers follow loop speed. Make the right path the fast path.

scenarios.title: The Golden Cage
scenarios.situation: The golden path covers 80% of services well. The remaining 20% — GPUs, exotic networking, legacy protocols — cannot use it at all, and the platform forbids exceptions.
choices: No paved exits: golden paths need documented escape hatches for legitimate exceptions. A path with no exits becomes a cage — advanced teams route around the entire platform, losing even the 80% value. The platform should serve the exceptions poorly-but-safely rather than forbid them.
The 20% should conform.
Golden paths should cover 100%.
Exceptions prove the platform failed.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Paved roads need off-ramps: the platform's contract should be 'the path handles the common cases; here is the supported way to diverge (with review).' Forbidding divergence does not produce conformity — it produces shadow infrastructure that gets none of the platform's benefits (security, observability). Graceful degradation of platform support beats rigid purity.
scenarios.hint: Where do the 20% go when the path forbids them?
evidence: Golden paths need documented escape hatches; cages breed shadows.

domains.name: Cloud Platforms
domains.summary: Landing zones, cloud networking, IAM, cost management, and multi-cloud strategy.

scenarios.title: The Single Account
scenarios.situation: A startup runs everything — prod, dev, experiments — in one cloud account. A developer testing a script deletes the production database 'because the names looked similar.'
choices: Better naming conventions.
More careful developers.
Ban scripts.

Account separation: prod, staging, dev, and sandbox in separate accounts — blast-radius isolation by construction, not by naming discipline. The developer's script cannot touch what its account cannot see. Naming conventions are not access control.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Blast radius must be structural: separate accounts make cross-environment damage impossible rather than merely discouraged. The incident's root cause was not carelessness but architecture — one account meant prod was always one command away. Account-per-boundary also buys cost attribution and policy scoping for free. 'Be more careful' is not a control; account boundaries are.
scenarios.hint: What would have made the deletion structurally impossible?
evidence: Prod/dev/sandbox in separate accounts. Names aren't access control.

scenarios.title: The Wildcard Admin
scenarios.situation: An audit finds a CI role with iam:* on * in production. It was created 'temporarily' two years ago for a migration.
choices: Immediate: scope it to the actions actually used (CloudTrail access advisor shows last-used), or delete if unused. Structural: permission boundaries capping what any role can grant, quarterly access reviews with removals, and a policy denying iam:* outside break-glass roles. 'Temporary' privilege is permanent until revoked.
Leave it; the migration might resume.
Delete it immediately with no analysis.
Wildcard is fine for CI.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. iam:* on * is privilege-escalation-as-a-service: anyone assuming the role can grant themselves anything. The remediation has two speeds: now (scope or delete using last-used data) and systemic (boundaries, reviews, deny rules). The 'temporary' origin is the pattern — every permanent over-privilege started as a shortcut. Reviews must remove, not just observe.
scenarios.hint: What could anyone assuming that role grant themselves?
evidence: Scope to last-used actions; boundaries cap grants; reviews remove.

scenarios.title: The $50k Surprise
scenarios.situation: Monday's bill shows $50,000 over the weekend: a misconfigured autoscaler spun up 400 GPU instances. Nobody noticed until finance called.
choices: Autoscaling is dangerous; use fixed capacity.

Layered cost controls: budget alerts per account/team (notify at 50/80/100%), anomaly detection on spend, and autoscaling guardrails (max instance counts, GPU quotas requiring approval). Cost anomalies are incidents — they deserve paging thresholds, not monthly reports.
Finance should check bills daily.
GPUs should be banned.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Cloud cost failures are control failures: no budget alert, no anomaly monitor, no scaling cap — three missing guardrails, any one of which would have caught it. The fix mirrors reliability practice: define the failure mode (spend spike), instrument it (budgets + anomaly detection), and cap the blast radius (quotas, max counts). 'Finance will notice' is not a control.
scenarios.hint: Which guardrail would have paged someone on Saturday?
evidence: Budgets, anomaly detection, scaling caps. Cost spikes are incidents.

scenarios.title: It's Always DNS
scenarios.situation: A service cannot reach its database after a VPC change. Security groups look right, routes look right, the database is healthy. Three hours are spent on firewall rules.
scenarios.prompt: What should have been checked first?
choices: Restart the database.
The VPC change was wrong; revert it.

DNS: private hosted zone resolution from the new VPC (resolver rules, zone associations). The symptom pattern — connectivity fails despite correct security groups and routes — is DNS-shaped: the name does not resolve, so no connection is ever attempted. 'It's always DNS' is a triage heuristic, not a joke.
More firewall rules.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. DNS is the most common hidden dependency: security groups and routes govern packets, but nothing sends packets to an unresolvable name. The triage order for connectivity is DNS → routing → security groups → application — checking resolution first (dig/nslookup from the affected host) would have saved three hours. VPC changes break zone associations silently; verify them explicitly.
scenarios.hint: Was any packet ever sent to the database?
evidence: Connectivity triage: DNS, then routing, then SGs. Check resolution first.

scenarios.title: The Quiet Exfiltration
scenarios.situation: Logs show large outbound transfers to an unknown IP every night from a workload with no business need for external access. It has been happening for months.
choices: Egress control and monitoring: workloads should have no internet route by default (private subnets, no NAT unless needed), with explicit egress allowlists and NAT/flow-log monitoring alerting on anomalous destinations. The workload's network shape should have made the transfer impossible, and monitoring should have caught it in days, not months.
A bigger firewall at the edge.
More antivirus.
The workload needed internet; allow it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D (index 3). The data-plane shape was wrong (unnecessary internet access) AND the monitoring was absent (months undetected). Defense in depth: default-no-egress subnets make exfiltration structurally hard; flow logs + anomaly detection catch what structure misses. Edge firewalls do not see workload-to-internet traffic as anomalous — only egress policy and monitoring do. 'No business need for external access' is the key phrase: the route should never have existed.
scenarios.hint: Why did the workload have an internet route at all?
evidence: Default no-internet for workloads; allowlist + monitor what leaves.

scenarios.title: The Lock-In Panic
scenarios.situation: Leadership demands multi-cloud 'to avoid lock-in,' with no specific service need. The platform team estimates 18 months of duplicated IAM, networking, and billing work.
choices: Cost the demand honestly: present the 18-month operational load against the specific lock-in risk (which workloads? what switching cost? what probability?), and propose the cheaper mitigations first — portable architectures (Kubernetes, Terraform, open formats) on one cloud. Multi-cloud is bought with permanent load; the purchase needs a named benefit.
Start building; leadership decided.
Refuse outright.
Do multi-cloud superficially to satisfy the demand.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 'Avoid lock-in' is a fear, not a requirement — the professional response translates it into priced options: the full multi-cloud build (18 months + permanent 2x load) vs portable-architecture mitigations (fraction of the cost, most of the benefit). Often the real risks (data gravity, proprietary services) have targeted answers. If leadership still chooses multi-cloud with eyes open, that is a legitimate business call — the failure is choosing it blind.
scenarios.hint: What specific risk does the 18-month build mitigate, and at what probability?
evidence: Price the permanent load against the named risk; try portability first.

scenarios.title: The Mystery Bill
scenarios.situation: $30k/month is unattributable — no tags, shared accounts, nobody claims it. Each team says 'not mine.'
choices: Delete everything untagged immediately.

Immediate: attribute via CloudTrail/resource inventory (who created what, when) and tag retroactively. Structural: mandatory tagging enforced by policy (deny untagged creates), tag-based cost allocation, and showback reports to owners monthly. Untagged resources should be undeployable, not just frowned upon.
Split the bill evenly.
Accept mystery spend as normal.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Unattributable spend is unmanageable spend: without ownership, nobody optimizes. The sequence is forensic (attribute what exists), preventive (policy denies untagged), and cultural (showback makes cost visible to owners). Deleting untagged resources immediately is tempting but risks production — quarantine and notify first. Tagging is the cheapest FinOps control and the most skipped.
scenarios.hint: Who optimizes spend that nobody owns?
evidence: Attribute, enforce at creation, showback to owners. Untagged = undeployable.

domains.name: Platform Security
domains.summary: Securing the platform: supply chain, secrets, zero trust, compliance, and runtime protection.

scenarios.title: The Poisoned Base
scenarios.situation: A popular base image is compromised upstream: new pulls include a cryptominer. Your builds use image: node:20 (mutable tag) with no verification.
choices: Pinned digests plus signature verification at admission: pinned digests mean you do not silently pull the poisoned update; cosign verification means even a pulled image cannot deploy without the publisher's valid signature. Either control breaks the chain; together they are defense in depth.
Faster incident response after deployment.
Banning open-source base images.
Hope the compromise is discovered quickly.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Mutable tags + no verification is the maximum-exposure posture: you automatically ingest upstream changes, including malicious ones, and nothing checks provenance before deploy. Pinning (digest) freezes what you consume; signatures (cosign) prove who produced it; admission enforces both at the cluster. The compromise still happened upstream — but it never reaches your workloads.
scenarios.hint: Would your pipeline have pulled the poisoned image automatically?
evidence: Digests freeze inputs; signatures prove provenance; admission enforces.

scenarios.title: The Git-Leaked Key
scenarios.situation: An AWS access key is committed to a public repo. It is discovered 6 hours later. The key had broad permissions.
choices: It was only 6 hours; probably fine.

Revoke first (kill the credential's power), then audit (CloudTrail: what did it do in 6 hours?), then rotate exposed resources, then structural fixes (secret scanning in pre-commit/CI, short-lived credentials, least privilege). Revocation before investigation — a live key is an ongoing breach.
Delete the commit from git history and move on.
Rotate the key next sprint.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The order matters: revoke stops the bleeding; audit scopes the damage; rotation cleans up; structural fixes prevent recurrence. Deleting git history does not unsee the key (scrapers copy in seconds) — revocation is the only containment. And 'probably fine' is not an incident conclusion; CloudTrail tells you what happened. Every leaked secret is two incidents: this one and the class.
scenarios.hint: What stops the bleeding: deleting history or revoking the key?
evidence: Revoke, audit, rotate, then fix the class. History deletion isn't containment.

scenarios.title: The Privileged Pod
scenarios.situation: A workload runs as root with privileged: true 'because the legacy app needs it.' It is compromised; the attacker escapes to the node.
choices: The app vendor is at fault; nothing to do.
Monitor privileged pods more closely.

Admission allowed an unjustifiable privilege: privileged containers disable all isolation — the compromise became a node compromise by design. The platform should deny privileged by policy (with a rare, expiring, reviewed exception process), and the app should be fixed or isolated (VM, not privileged pod). 'Needs it' is not a security argument.
Kubernetes is insecure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. privileged: true removes the container boundary — it is root on the host with all capabilities. Allowing it by default means every workload compromise is a node compromise. Policy (OPA/Kyverno deny) should block it; exceptions need expiry, review, and compensating controls. Monitoring a privileged pod is watching a loaded gun — the fix is unloading it.
scenarios.hint: What does privileged: true remove?
evidence: privileged:true = no container boundary. Deny by policy; exceptions expire.

scenarios.title: The Spoofed Service
scenarios.situation: Service A trusts requests from service B by source IP. An attacker in the cluster spoofs the IP and calls A's admin endpoint.
choices: Block the attacker's IP.
IPs are fine; the attacker was sophisticated.
Put A and B in separate clusters.

Mutual TLS with workload identity: both sides present cryptographic identities (SPIFFE/IRSA), verified per request — not IPs, which are spoofable and reassignable. The admin endpoint should additionally require authorization (policy per identity), not just authentication.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. IP-based trust confuses addressing with identity: IPs change, are shared (NAT), and are spoofable within the network. Workload identity (certificates bound to the service account) is unforgeable by network position. mTLS gives both encryption and mutual authentication; authorization policy then decides what the authenticated identity may do. 'Trust the network' died with the perimeter.
scenarios.hint: Is an IP an identity?
evidence: mTLS with workload identity. IPs are addresses, spoofable and shared.

scenarios.title: The Audit Scramble
scenarios.situation: Every year, the team spends six weeks assembling compliance evidence: screenshots, spreadsheets, and frantic log searches. Findings repeat annually.
choices: The frameworks are the problem.

Continuous compliance: controls as code (policies evaluated on every change), evidence as a byproduct (immutable logs of passing checks), and quarterly control reviews. The audit becomes an export, not a project. Repeating findings mean the controls are not operating — fix the operation, not the evidence.
Hire audit-prep consultants annually.
More screenshots, better organized.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A (index 0). The scramble is the symptom: controls that only exist at audit time do not exist. Continuous compliance inverts the model — every deploy proves the controls held, and the evidence accumulates automatically. Repeating findings are the tell: the same gap, found yearly, never fixed systemically. The fix is operational (automate the control), not documentary (better screenshots).
scenarios.hint: Were the controls operating in March, or only in audit month?
evidence: Controls as code, evidence as byproduct. Audit = export, not project.

scenarios.title: The Shell in the Container
scenarios.situation: Runtime detection alerts: a shell spawned in a container whose image contains no shell and whose app never shells. The securityContext allowed it.
scenarios.prompt: What does the alert mean, and what is the hardening?
choices: Containers always have shells; ignore it.

Likely compromise or exploitation: unexpected process execution in a minimal container is the classic intrusion signal. Hardening: distroless/scratch images (no shell to spawn), read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities, seccomp — and treat the alert as an incident (isolate, capture, investigate), not noise.
The alert is a false positive; tune it out.
Install a shell for debugging convenience.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. In a minimal image, a shell appearing is anomalous by construction — that is the point of minimal images: they make intrusion visible. The response is incident response (the container is untrusted until proven otherwise), and the hardening removes the attacker's tools (no shell, no write, no privilege). Detection and hardening are complements: hardening raises the bar, detection catches what clears it.
scenarios.hint: Why is a shell anomalous in this container?
evidence: Minimal images make intrusion visible. Unexpected shell = incident.

scenarios.title: The Mystery Dependency
scenarios.situation: A critical CVE is announced in a popular library. Leadership asks: 'are we affected?' The team spends three days inventorying services by hand.
choices: Fewer dependencies.
The CVE database is too slow.
