SBOMs (software bills of materials) for every artifact, queryable centrally: the answer should be a query ('which images contain lib X at version < Y?'), not an archaeology project. SBOMs are generated at build time, stored with the artifact, and indexed — vulnerability response becomes search, not excavation.
Faster engineers.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Vulnerability response time is dominated by inventory time: knowing what you run, where. SBOMs make the software supply chain queryable — the three-day manual inventory becomes a thirty-second query. Generation is cheap (syft at build); the value compounds at every CVE. 'Are we affected?' is the question SBOMs exist to answer.
scenarios.hint: How long should 'are we affected?' take to answer?
evidence: Every artifact gets a bill of materials. CVE response = query, not dig.

domains.name: GitOps Workflows
domains.summary: Git as the source of truth: principles, agents, drift handling, promotion strategies, and recovery.

scenarios.title: The CI Credential Heist
scenarios.situation: CI pushes to production with a cluster-admin kubeconfig stored in CI secrets. An attacker compromises a CI runner and extracts it.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the push model the vulnerability, and what is the fix?
choices: Use a weaker kubeconfig in CI.

Push requires production credentials in CI — the most-exposed system holds the most-powerful secret. The pull model inverts it: the in-cluster agent pulls from git, CI never touches the cluster, and there is no kubeconfig to steal. The attack surface shrinks to the agent's scoped permissions.
CI runners are inherently insecure; avoid CI.
Rotate the kubeconfig monthly.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The push model's flaw is architectural: credentials must live where the pushing happens (CI), and CI is exposed (runs untrusted code, broad access). Pull removes the credential from CI entirely — the cluster reaches out to git, which needs no cluster credentials. Rotation and weaker keys mitigate; pull eliminates the class.
scenarios.hint: Where do production cluster credentials live in each model?
evidence: Agents pull; CI never holds cluster credentials. Smaller attack surface.

scenarios.title: The Midnight Edit
scenarios.situation: An engineer kubectl-edits a production deployment at midnight to stop an incident, then goes to sleep. Morning: the agent reverted the edit (self-heal), and the incident's mitigation is gone.
choices: The agent is too aggressive.
Midnight edits should be forbidden.

The emergency edit never became a git commit: GitOps discipline requires every cluster change to be committed within the hour — the agent did its job (enforcing git as truth); the human broke the contract. The fix is process: emergency edits are followed by immediate PRs, or the mitigation evaporates.
Self-heal should be disabled.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Self-heal worked as designed — the failure was the missing commit. This is the GitOps social contract: the cluster is a cache of git, and any write not in git is temporary by definition. The runbook for emergency edits must end with 'open the PR' — the incident is not mitigated until the mitigation is in git. Disabling self-heal treats the symptom (and surrenders drift correction).
scenarios.hint: Was the mitigation ever durable?
evidence: Every cluster edit becomes a git commit within the hour, or it evaporates.

scenarios.title: The Unreviewed Promotion
scenarios.situation: Someone edits the prod image tag directly in git, bypassing PR review ('it's just a tag'). The tag points to an untested artifact; production breaks.
choices: Tags should be longer.
Trust the team more.
The artifact was bad; test harder.

Branch protection on the GitOps repo: promotion = PR = review + CI checks (policy, diff, test evidence). 'Just a tag' is the deploy — it deserves the same rigor as a code change, because it IS the deploy. Direct pushes to the deployment repo must be mechanically impossible.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. In GitOps, the git write is the deployment action — it needs the deployment's controls: review, automated checks, audit trail. Branch protection makes the process mechanical, not cultural: the direct push is rejected by the system, not frowned upon by peers. The tag's content (untested artifact) is a separate failure — promotion gates should also verify test evidence, not just syntax.
scenarios.hint: In GitOps, what IS the deploy?
evidence: Git writes are deploys: protect branches, require review + checks.

scenarios.title: The Noisy Drift
scenarios.situation: Drift alerts fire constantly: the HPA changes replica counts, and every change shows as drift. The team mutes the drift channel.
choices: ignoreDifferences for HPA-managed fields: the diff should show human-meaningful divergence, not controller noise. Excluding /spec/replicas (owned by the HPA) restores the alert's signal — every remaining drift alert means a human did something. Muting was the symptom; noisy diffs were the disease.
Disable the HPA.
Delete the drift alerts.
Set replicas manually.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Drift detection must distinguish human writes from controller writes: autoscalers, operators, and finalizers legitimately mutate resources, and diffing their fields produces false positives that train teams to ignore the channel. ignoreDifferences tunes the diff to intent — git owns the declared shape, controllers own their fields. The muted channel was a monitoring failure caused by a tuning failure.
scenarios.hint: Who owns the replica count: git or the HPA?
evidence: ignoreDifferences for controller-owned fields. Drift alerts must mean human action.

scenarios.title: The Untested Restore
scenarios.situation: The DR plan says 'reconverge from git.' It has never been tested. During a real region outage, the team discovers the git repo lacks the sealed-secrets keys and the data backups are untested.
choices: The region outage was unforeseeable.
More documentation would have saved them.

Config recovery without its secrets (sealed-secrets keys, external secret stores must be recoverable independently) and data recovery without tested restores (snapshots exist but restore was never practiced). GitOps covers stateless config beautifully; secrets and data are the separate halves that need their own drills and measured RTOs.
GitOps doesn't work for DR.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B (index 1). The failure was untested assumptions: the plan assumed secrets and data would be there, but neither half was drilled. DR has three recoveries — config (git, easy), secrets (keys/stores, often forgotten), data (snapshots, hard). Each needs its own drill and measured RTO. 'Reconverge from git' is one third of a DR plan.
scenarios.hint: What three things must be recoverable, and which were drilled?
evidence: Config (git) + secrets (keys) + data (tested restores). Drill all three.

scenarios.title: The Monorepo Blast Radius
scenarios.situation: One giant GitOps repo syncs everything to every cluster. A bad commit to a dev app's config triggers a full-cluster resync that restarts production workloads.
choices: One repo is fine; be careful.
Stop using GitOps.

Smaller sync units: per-team or per-app repos (or well-scoped paths with per-app Applications), so a change's blast radius is its own app. The sync unit is the failure unit — giant units mean giant failures. Directories-per-env within a repo still need per-app Application boundaries.
Bigger commits, less often.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The sync unit defines the failure domain: whatever syncs together can break together. Per-application (or per-team) repos/paths with separate Application resources isolate changes — a dev app's bad config cannot resync prod. This mirrors the account/cluster separation logic: boundaries must be structural, not aspirational. 'Be careful' is not a blast-radius control.
scenarios.hint: What is the failure unit of a sync?
evidence: The sync unit is the failure unit. Isolate apps/teams.

scenarios.title: The Auditor's Question
scenarios.situation: An auditor asks: 'Who deployed version 1.4.2 to production, when, and was it approved?'
choices: Check CI logs from that week.
Ask in chat who remembers.
The auditor should trust the team.

From git history: the promotion PR shows the author, timestamp, reviewers, CI checks (policy, tests), and the exact diff (tag 1.4.1 → 1.4.2). The deployment's audit trail is the version control history — complete, immutable, and queryable. No separate deployment log needed.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. GitOps makes deployment auditability a property of the version control system: every production change is a reviewed commit with author, timestamp, approvers, and automated check results. This is why regulated industries adopt GitOps — the compliance evidence is generated as a side effect of the normal workflow, not assembled afterward. 'Who deployed?' becomes git log.
scenarios.hint: Where is the deployment's audit trail?
evidence: Promotion PRs = who/when/approved. Compliance as a side effect.

domains.name: SRE Practices
domains.summary: The SRE discipline: error budgets in action, toil elimination, capacity planning, chaos engineering, and learning from failure.

scenarios.title: The Ticket Treadmill
scenarios.situation: The SRE team spends 70% of its time on manual tickets: provisioning, access grants, deploy assists. Engineering projects stall; toil grows with every new service.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis and prescription?
choices: The team needs better time management.
Toil is the job; accept it.

Toil exceeding the 50% cap with no elimination plan: prescribe toil accounting (measure by category), then elimination projects per category — self-service for provisioning, automation for deploys — each with the reclaimed hours as its ROI. Past 50% toil, the team is ops; the fix is structural, not motivational.
Hire more SREs to handle tickets.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The 50% rule exists because toil scales with success: every new service adds tickets, so ticket-handling headcount is a treadmill. The only exit is elimination — automation or removal — measured by the toil ledger. Hiring into toil grows the treadmill; the reclaimed-hours ROI makes elimination projects fundable. 'Better time management' cannot beat arithmetic.
scenarios.hint: Does handling tickets faster reduce next month's tickets?
evidence: Max 50% on toil. Measure by category; eliminate with automation.

scenarios.title: The Launch Meltdown
scenarios.situation: A marketing launch drives 10x traffic. The autoscaler was never tested at that scale; it hits quota limits and scale-up takes 8 minutes. The site is down for 20 minutes.
scenarios.prompt: What was missing from capacity planning?
choices: Bigger instances.
Marketing should not launch.
Autoscaling does not work.

Tested scaling: autoscaling configured but never load-tested at projected peak, quota headroom never verified, scale-up latency never measured. Capacity planning is assumption management — every untested assumption (quota, speed, headroom) is a latent incident. The load test would have found all three cheaply.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The autoscaler existed but its assumptions were untested: quota caps, scale-up speed, and headroom at 10x. Load testing at projected peak is how capacity plans get verified — the test finds the quota limit in staging instead of the outage finding it in production. 'We have autoscaling' without 'we tested it at 10x' is the capacity version of the untested rollback.
scenarios.hint: Which assumptions were tested before the launch?
evidence: Load-test at projected peak. Untested autoscaling is untested capacity.

scenarios.title: The Vandalism Objection
scenarios.situation: Leadership hears 'chaos engineering' and says: 'You want to break production on purpose? Absolutely not.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you make the case?
choices: Reframe as hypothesis testing with abort conditions: start in staging with tiny blast radius, state the falsifiable belief ('zone loss shifts traffic in 60s'), define auto-abort on SLO breach, and show the findings become fixes. It is the scientific method applied to resilience — and the alternative is discovering the weakness during a real outage.
Do it secretly without telling anyone.
Agree; chaos is reckless.
Start with the biggest possible failure to prove the point.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The objection confuses chaos engineering with random breakage; the answer is the experiment card — hypothesis, tiny blast radius, abort conditions, follow-up tickets. Starting small with measured results builds the trust for larger experiments. And the alternative framing is honest: every untested assumption is an experiment too, just one run by reality at the worst time.
scenarios.hint: Is the assumption tested by you in staging, or by reality at 3 AM?
evidence: State the belief, bound the blast radius, abort on breach.

scenarios.title: The Third Identical Incident
scenarios.situation: The same certificate-expiry outage happens for the third time. Each postmortem said 'add monitoring.' Nobody did.
choices: Some incidents just repeat.

Action items without ownership and follow-through: postmortems that produce unowned wishes instead of tracked work. The fix is systemic — max 5 actions, each owned and dated, tracked like product work, with repeat-incident tagging that escalates the category. The third identical incident is amnesia, not bad luck.
Certificates are hard.
The postmortems were wrong.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Repeat incidents are the metric of learning failure: the organization paid the tuition (the outage) but skipped the class (the fix). Unowned action items are wishes; repeat tagging makes the pattern visible and escalatable. cert-manager (automation) would have eliminated the category entirely — the deepest fix is removing the manual step, not monitoring it better.
scenarios.hint: What happened to the action items from incident #2?
evidence: Max 5, owned, dated, tracked. Repeats = process failure.

scenarios.title: The Impossible SLO
scenarios.situation: Product demands 99.99% for a service built on a 99.9% dependency. Engineering says it is impossible without a rewrite.
scenarios.prompt: How should SRE handle the negotiation?
choices: Promise 99.99% and hope.
Refuse; SRE sets SLOs unilaterally.
The dependency will improve on its own.

Make the cost visible: 99.99% allows 52 minutes/year downtime; the dependency alone consumes 8.7 hours — the math proves impossibility, not opinion. Then offer options: lower the SLO, fund the rewrite, or add redundancy (with its price tag). The SLO is a business decision with a cost; SRE's job is pricing it, not wishing it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C (index 2). SLO negotiation is arithmetic, not advocacy: dependency math (the product of availabilities) sets the ceiling, and the gap between demand and reality has a price (redundancy, rewrite). Presenting options with costs turns the standoff into a business decision — which is what SLOs are. 'Hope' is not a reliability strategy; unilateral refusal is not a partnership.
scenarios.hint: What does the dependency math allow: 99.99% or 99.9%?
evidence: Dependencies set the ceiling. Price the gap; let the business choose.

scenarios.title: The Skipped Pre-Mortem
scenarios.situation: A launch fails on the exact failure mode one engineer privately predicted but never voiced ('I didn't want to be negative').
scenarios.prompt: What practice would have caught it, and why does it work?
choices: The engineer should be braver.
Postmortems would have caught it.
Launches always have surprises; accept it.

Pre-mortem: assuming the failure as fact unlocks candor — 'it's 3 months later, we failed, why?' lets people voice doubts without seeming negative. The private prediction becomes a shared mitigation. Cultures that punish 'negativity' need the structure that makes doubt safe.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The failure was social, not technical: the knowledge existed but the culture suppressed it. Pre-mortems work by changing the social frame — imagining failure as already-fact makes raising risks helpful rather than negative. 'Be braver' asks individuals to fight culture; the pre-mortem changes the culture's default. Psychological safety is a process output, not a poster.
scenarios.hint: Why didn't the engineer speak up?
evidence: Assume failure as fact; unlock candor. Structure beats bravery.

scenarios.title: The Efficiency Trap
scenarios.situation: Finance pushes for 95% utilization: 'idle capacity is waste.' SRE wants 65% for headroom. Both claim efficiency.
choices: Price the headroom as insurance: at 95%, any spike or single failure becomes an incident — the 'waste' is the premium for absorbing variance. Show the incident cost of the last capacity crunch vs the infrastructure savings. Efficiency without resilience is fragility with good metrics.
Finance is right; maximize utilization.
SRE is right; ignore finance.
Split the difference at 80%.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The dispute is about the price of variance: 95% utilization is efficient only in a world without spikes or failures — i.e., not this world. The resolution is economic: quantify the last capacity incident's cost (downtime, toil, reputation) against the headroom's price. Headroom is insurance; argue it like insurance — with the claim history, not with principles.
scenarios.hint: What does 95% utilization cost when the spike comes?
evidence: Utilization targets price variance. Show the claim history.

domains.name: Exam & Interview Prep
domains.summary: How platform engineering is hired: system design interviews, troubleshooting scenarios, behavioral rounds, and a study plan.

scenarios.title: Design a CI/CD Platform
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Design a CI/CD platform for 200 engineers and 50 services. You have 45 minutes.'
choices: 'I'd use Jenkins because I know it.'
Start drawing boxes immediately.
Ask for the 'right answer' hint.

Clarify before designing: deploys per day, environments, compliance needs, current pain, non-goals — then sketch. Requirements you assume are requirements you get wrong; the questions themselves demonstrate seniority. Jumping to 'I'd use X tool' is the classic junior fail.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. System design interviews grade structured thinking under ambiguity: the clarification phase (10 min) prevents solving the wrong problem and shows stakeholder instincts. Tool-first answers reveal tool-shaped thinking; trade-off discussions ('why this over that, given THEIR constraints') reveal engineering. The interviewer has no single right answer — they have a rubric for method.
scenarios.hint: What do you not yet know that would change the design?
evidence: Requirements before boxes. Questions demonstrate seniority.

scenarios.title: The Live Debug
scenarios.situation: Interviewer shares a terminal: 'Checkout is down. Debug it live.' You have no idea where to start.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first move?
choices: Restate the symptom and state your method aloud: 'Checkout errors started when? Let me check the deploy history and error metrics first — recent changes are the most likely cause.' Narrated, hypothesis-driven, cheapest-test-first. Silence plus random commands is the fail mode.
Start running commands quickly to look competent.
Ask for the answer.
Reboot everything.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Live debugging grades method, not knowledge: restating shows listening, hypotheses show structure, cheapest-first shows judgment, narration shows communication. Base rates (recent changes cause most incidents) guide the first move. Interviewers forgive wrong hypotheses; they do not forgive flailing — because flailing is what fails real incidents.
scenarios.hint: What does the interviewer grade: the fix or the method?
evidence: Hypothesis -> cheapest test -> observe. Say every step.

scenarios.title: The Trade-Off Question
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'You chose canary over blue-green. Defend it.'
choices: Refuse to choose.

Contextual trade-offs: 'For this service, canary wins because error metrics are well-defined and traffic is high enough for statistical signal; blue-green would be better for stateful/schema changes where instant rollback matters. I'd revisit if traffic drops.' Trade-offs are contextual — strong answers name the conditions, not just the winner.
'Canary is best practice.'
'Blue-green is outdated.'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. 'Defend it' tests trade-off reasoning: the strong answer names what each option optimizes, states the conditions favoring the choice, and names when you'd switch. 'Best practice' answers reveal memorization; conditional answers reveal judgment. Seniority in interviews is almost entirely this: comfort with 'it depends, and here is what it depends on.'
scenarios.hint: Under what conditions would you switch your choice?
evidence: 'It depends' + the conditions. Name when you'd switch.

scenarios.title: Tell Me About a Mistake
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Tell me about a technical mistake you made.'
choices: 'I've never made a serious mistake.'
A mistake with no lesson.

Full ownership plus systemic fix: 'I deleted the wrong database (mine); the fix wasn't being careful — it was adding confirmation prompts and backups to the tooling, which I then built. Now I check what systems allow mistakes, not just my attention.' Owned failure with a systemic fix and a changed practice.
A mistake that was actually someone else's fault.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The mistake question tests accountability and learning: everyone has caused incidents; the hireable signal is owning it and fixing the system that allowed it. Blame-shifting fails instantly; 'no mistakes' fails credibility. The systemic fix is the key — it shows the candidate thinks in systems, which is the entire job.
scenarios.hint: Did you fix yourself or the system?
evidence: Full ownership + systemic fix + changed practice.

scenarios.title: The Scale Question
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Your design works for 50 services. What breaks at 500?'
choices: Scaling reasoning: which components become bottlenecks (the single CI queue? the monorepo sync? the manual approval?), what changes qualitatively (need sharding, federation, self-service), and what you would monitor to see it coming. 'What breaks' is the senior lens — juniors describe the happy path; seniors describe the failure modes at 10x.
Whether you know big numbers.
Optimism about the design.
Nothing; it's a trick.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D (index 3). The scale question separates architecture from architecture-at-scale: bottlenecks (queues, single writers, manual gates), qualitative changes (federation, sharding, automation replacing humans), and leading indicators. Strong answers name the first three things that break and the redesign each forces. It is the same skill as capacity planning — applied to the interview whiteboard.
scenarios.hint: What breaks first at 10x, and what does that force?
evidence: Name what breaks at 10x and the redesign each break forces.

scenarios.title: Why Platform Engineering?
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Why platform engineering, rather than product engineering or SRE?'
choices: Specificity about the leverage: 'I like multiplying other engineers' effectiveness — the toil I killed saved 40h/week across teams, and platform work compounds. Product engineering optimizes one product; platform optimizes the org's ability to ship.' Concrete leverage story, not generic enthusiasm.
'I like Kubernetes.'
'It pays well.'
'I couldn't decide.'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 'Why this role' tests self-knowledge and fit: the credible answer names the specific satisfaction (leverage, multiplication, systems thinking) with evidence (the toil killed, the path built). Generic answers ('I like tech') fit any role and therefore none. The interviewer is asking: will this person be energized by our work in month six?
scenarios.hint: What energizes you about platform work specifically?
evidence: Name the leverage with evidence. Generic enthusiasm fits no role.

scenarios.title: The Disagreement Story
scenarios.situation: Interviewer: 'Tell me about a technical disagreement with a colleague.'
choices: Whether you avoid disagreement.

How you handle conflict: did you seek the data (prototype, metrics), steelman their position, and converge on the merits — or escalate, concede resentfully, or win politically? The story's arc should be: disagreement → joint investigation → better decision (whoever's it was) → relationship intact.
Whether you usually win arguments.
For gossip about the colleague.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Disagreement stories test collaboration under conflict: the signal is epistemics (how did you decide who was right?) and relationship (did the working relationship survive?). Strong stories show steelmanning, empirical resolution, and graceful concession. 'I convinced them' is fine if the mechanism was evidence; 'my manager decided' reveals nothing.
scenarios.hint: How did you decide who was right?
evidence: Steelman, test empirically, concede gracefully. Show the mechanism.

domains.name: Mock Assessment: Timed Trial
domains.description: A timed, mixed-domain final assessment simulating interview conditions: system design, troubleshooting, and trade-off questions from every domain. Take it mid-course as a diagnostic and again at the end.

lessons.title: Platform Engineering — Core concepts
concepts: An Internal Developer Platform is a product: curated tools, APIs, and workflows that let developers self-serve infrastructure. Kubernetes and CI are building blocks; the IDP is the productized layer with developers as customers.
The software catalog is the platform's front door. Minimum viable entry: name, owner, lifecycle stage, repo and runbook links — ownership first, rich metadata later.

Golden paths are paved roads, not mandates: the blessed way to build, test, and ship, maintained and secure by default, with escape hatches for justified exceptions. Adoption comes from being the easiest path.
Software templates scaffold new services consistently, but each template is a maintenance liability — consolidate to a few parameterized templates with versioning and deprecation.
Platform APIs wrap slow operations asynchronously: 202 Accepted with an operation ID, pollable status, and structured actionable errors — because the caller is usually automation.

example.code:
curl -s https://platform.example.com/api/v1/templates | jq '.[].name'
curl -s -X POST https://platform.example.com/api/v1/environments \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"service": "checkout", "type": "preview"}' | jq .operation_id
example.walkthrough: Discover available templates, then request an ephemeral preview environment asynchronously — the API returns an operation ID immediately and you poll for completion instead of holding a 20-minute HTTP connection.

pitfalls: Common trap: measuring platform success by features shipped — measure developer outcomes (time-to-deploy, ticket deflection, adoption).
Common trap: mandating the golden path — mandates breed shadow IT; make it the easiest path instead.
Common trap: 40 near-identical templates — every template multiplies CVE patch work.
Common trap: synchronous platform APIs for minute-long operations — proxies and clients will time out.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Platform Engineering move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Platform Engineering
concepts: Platform Engineering is a multi-step process within Platform Engineering: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Platform Engineering to the broader Platform Engineering ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

example.code:
Step 1: Initiation
  Platform Engineering begins — what triggers it?

Step 2: Processing
  Data flows through — what transforms it?

Step 3: Handoff
  Result passes to next system — what is the interface?

Step 4: Completion
  Final state reached — how do you verify?
example.walkthrough: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Platform Engineering. Draw it as a flowing sequence, not a static diagram.

pitfalls: Treating Platform Engineering as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists
lessons.try_it: Whiteboard the full Platform Engineering flow from memory. Label every handoff and dependency.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp is organized as domains (major areas). Each domain holds lessons (concept briefings), scenarios (graded incident and design decisions), and labs (hands-on terminal exercises with self-checks).

The intended loop: read a lesson, attempt its scenarios closed-book, then do the lab in a terminal. Platform engineering is a doing discipline — reading about Kubernetes never taught anyone Kubernetes.
Scenarios simulate the decisions you will face on the job and in interviews: outages, design trade-offs, prioritization. Every wrong choice names a real anti-pattern.
The mock-assessment domain is a timed final; capstone-build guides you to ship a working internal developer platform slice end to end.

example.code:
A 90-minute study block:
  0:00-0:20  read the lesson; sketch the architecture by hand
  0:20-0:45  scenarios closed-book, committing to each answer
  0:45-1:20  lab in a real terminal (local kind cluster or VM)
  1:20-1:30  error log: one line per miss, revisit weekly
example.walkthrough: Hand-sketching architectures before touching YAML builds the mental model that makes manifests readable. The error log converts each miss into a revisit target.

pitfalls: Reading without a terminal open — platform skills are muscle memory.
Peeking at answers before committing. The commitment is the training.
Skipping labs because the concepts 'made sense.' Recognition is not production.
lessons.try_it: Provision a local kind cluster today; you will need it for every lab in this course.

lessons.title: Your Study Strategy: Systems-First Learning
concepts: Learn bottom-up: Linux processes, networking, and DNS before Kubernetes; Kubernetes before GitOps; GitOps before platform abstractions. Every layer demystifies the one above it.
One concept, one terminal proof: after each lesson, prove the concept with a command (create the pod, break the probe, watch the restart). Unproven concepts evaporate.
Interleave domains: study observability alongside Kubernetes — the exam and the job mix them, so your practice should too.
Keep an incident ledger: every scenario miss becomes a one-line entry (confused distinction + fix). Review it before each lab session.

example.code:
Incident-ledger entry:
  CONFUSED: liveness vs readiness probes
  FIX: liveness = restart me; readiness = remove me from service
  PROOF: kubectl describe pod after failed readiness -> no restart,
          just Endpoints removal
example.walkthrough: The ledger plus terminal proofs is the whole method: each miss becomes a command you have actually run. Interviewers can tell read knowledge from run knowledge in one follow-up question.

pitfalls: Top-down learning: starting with service meshes before understanding TCP. The layers will punish you.
Collecting tools instead of concepts. Tools churn; the control loop, the probe, the SLO persist.
Studying without breaking things. The lab that never fails teaches nothing about failure.
lessons.try_it: Write your first incident-ledger entry after the orientation scenarios.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap: The Thirteen Domains
concepts: Foundations arc: kubernetes-platform, cicd-pipelines, and infrastructure-as-code build the core substrate every platform stands on.
Operations arc: observability-sre, sre-practices, and platform-security cover running things reliably and safely — the 'day 2' that interviews probe hardest.
Product arc: developer-experience, gitops-workflows, and cloud-platforms cover the platform as a product — golden paths, self-service, landing zones.
Capstone arc: pe-exam-prep collects interview strategy (system design, troubleshooting, behavioral); mock-assessment is the timed trial; capstone-build ships a real platform slice.

example.code:
Roadmap:
  start-here -> kubernetes-platform -> cicd-pipelines -> infrastructure-as-code
      -> observability-sre -> sre-practices -> platform-security
      -> developer-experience -> gitops-workflows -> cloud-platforms
      -> pe-exam-prep -> mock-assessment -> capstone-build
example.walkthrough: Follow the foundations first: GitOps makes no sense without declarative state, and SLOs make no sense without the failure modes of the substrate. The order is load-bearing.

pitfalls: Jumping to GitOps before understanding declarative Kubernetes state.
Treating security as a final chapter. It constrains every earlier decision — read it in parallel.
Saving the mock for 'when ready.' Take it early as a diagnostic.
lessons.try_it: Mark the two domains you know least and schedule them first — weakness-first ordering.

lessons.title: Labs, Scenarios, and the Mock Assessment
concepts: Labs give steps plus checks: the checks are command patterns your terminal output should match (e.g., a pod in Running state, a metric name in Prometheus). They are self-verification, not auto-graders.
Scenarios carry objectives (what is tested), mins (budget like an interview), evidence (the reference fact), and a hint. Commit to an answer before reading the hint.
The mock assessment simulates interview pressure: mixed-domain questions, no hints, strict time. Take it twice — mid-course as a diagnostic, once at the end.
The capstone ships a real slice: a service template with CI, GitOps delivery, dashboards, and docs — the artifact you demo in interviews.

example.code:
Mock protocol:
  120 minutes, no notes, domains mixed
  -> score -> log every miss in the incident ledger
  -> re-study only the missed distinctions
  -> rebuild the failed lab commands by hand
example.walkthrough: Two timed runs lift performance more than a week of re-reading, because they train retrieval and selection under pressure — the actual interview conditions.

pitfalls: Using hints as a first resort.
Treating the capstone as optional. It is the interview artifact — the highest-ROI domain.
Reviewing only correct answers. The misses are the curriculum.
lessons.try_it: Do one lab from the Kubernetes domain today to feel the format before you need it under pressure.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 1 — Service Template and Local Platform
concepts: Pick the slice: one service template (e.g., a Python API) that scaffolds a repo with Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, CI pipeline, and README — the golden path's minimum viable product.
Define 'done' for phase 1: `scaffold new-service` produces a repo that builds, tests, and deploys to a local kind cluster with one command. If it takes more than one command, it is not a golden path.
Keep the template boring: pinned base images, non-root user, health endpoints, structured logging, resource requests/limits. Boring is the feature — every clever choice is support load.
Version the template and test it in CI: the template repo has its own pipeline that scaffolds a test service and deploys it. Templates rot; test them like code.

example.code:
scaffold.yaml (template descriptor):
  name: python-api
  version: 1.3.0
  files:
    - Dockerfile          # pinned base, non-root, tini init
    - k8s/deployment.yaml # probes, resources, HPA hooks
    - .ci/pipeline.yaml   # lint -> test -> build -> scan -> push
    - README.md           # runbook + ownership
example.walkthrough: The template descriptor is a contract: it promises every scaffolded service ships with the platform's standards built in. Versioning it lets you roll out standard changes (new base image) to all future services.

pitfalls: Building the template for every language at once. One golden path, proven, then expand.
Clever base images (distroless before you need it). Boring first, optimize later.
Untested templates. A template that rots poisons every service scaffolded from it.
lessons.try_it: Write the 'done' checklist for your phase 1; every item must be verifiable by a command.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 2 — CI, GitOps Delivery, and Guardrails
concepts: Wire the pipeline: lint, unit test, build image, scan (vulnerabilities + secrets), push to registry, update the GitOps repo with the new image tag. Every step is a gate; a failed gate stops the line.

GitOps delivery: the cluster state lives in a git repo; an agent (Argo CD/Flux pattern) syncs it. Developers merge to main; the agent deploys. No kubectl from laptops to production — the git history IS the audit log.
Add the guardrails: branch protection, required reviews, image signature verification, policy checks (no :latest, resources required, non-root). Guardrails make the safe path the easy path.
Prove the rollback: deploy a bad version, watch the pipeline's gates or the GitOps revert restore service. A delivery system without a proven rollback is a hope, not a system.

example.code:
promotion flow:
  dev:  auto-sync from main (fast feedback)
  stage: manual promotion (promote.yaml PR)
  prod:  manual promotion + required checks
           (SLOs green, security scan clean)
  rollback: git revert of the promotion commit
example.walkthrough: Promotion as git operations gives you auditability, review, and rollback for free — the version control system becomes the deployment system. This is the GitOps insight in one paragraph.

pitfalls: Auto-sync to production. Speed without gates is just faster incidents.
kubectl from laptops. Every manual cluster write is unaudited drift.
Unproven rollbacks. The rollback you have not tested does not exist.
lessons.try_it: Draw your promotion flow; mark every gate and who approves each promotion.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 3 — Observability, Docs, and Demo
concepts: Instrument the template: every scaffolded service emits RED metrics (rate, errors, duration), structured logs, and traces — with dashboards and alerts provisioned automatically, not hand-built per service.
Write the docs a new hire needs: 5-minute quickstart, architecture diagram, runbook for the top three failure modes, ownership and escalation. Docs are part of the platform, not an afterthought.
Measure the platform: time-to-first-deploy for a new service, lead time for changes, failed-deployment rate. These are your platform's SLOs — report them like a product.
Demo it end to end: scaffold, commit, watch CI, watch GitOps sync, break it, watch alerts fire, roll back. The demo IS the interview artifact — record it.

example.code:
Demo script (15 minutes):
  0:00 scaffold new service (one command)
  0:02 push; watch CI gates pass
  0:05 GitOps syncs to stage; dashboards populate
  0:08 deploy bad version; alert fires; SLO burn visible
  0:11 git revert; service recovers
  0:14 docs: runbook predicted this exact failure
example.walkthrough: The demo's narrative arc — build, ship, break, detect, recover — is the whole platform story in fifteen minutes. Interviewers remember narratives, not architectures.

pitfalls: Hand-built dashboards per service. Provision from the template or drown in toil.
Docs written last and never. Docs are the platform's UI for humans.
Vanity metrics (number of services). Measure outcomes: lead time, reliability, toil.
lessons.try_it: Record the 15-minute demo; watch it once and cut everything that is not build-ship-break-recover.

lessons.title: Platform Engineering — The Platform as a Product
concepts: Treat the platform as a product and developers as customers: roadmaps, user research, adoption metrics, and support. Platforms built as side projects die as side projects.
The platform team topology question: platform teams enable stream-aligned teams (Team Topologies) — they do not own the product's runtime. Confusing enablement with ownership creates bottlenecks.

Thinnest viable platform: start with the smallest thing that removes the biggest pain (usually CI + paved deploy path), then expand by measured demand. Big-bang platforms collapse under their own scope.
Internal marketing matters: golden paths only work if discovered. Demos, office hours, and migration assistance are product work, not overhead.

example.code:
TVP canvas:
  BIGGEST PAIN: deploys take 2 weeks and a ticket queue
  THINNEST FIX: pipeline template + one-command deploy to dev
  MEASURE: lead time before/after for 3 pilot teams
  EXPAND ONLY IF: lead time drops and teams ask for more
example.walkthrough: The product framing changes every decision: 'which feature next?' becomes 'which developer pain is biggest?' — answered by research, not by architecture astronauts.

pitfalls: Building the platform developers deserve instead of the one they asked for. Research first.
Platform team as ticket queue. Enablement means self-service, not a new silo.
Big-bang scope. If phase 1 takes 9 months, phase 1 is wrong.
lessons.try_it: Interview three developers about their biggest infrastructure pain; rank the answers.

lessons.title: Platform Engineering — Self-Service Without Anarchy
concepts: Self-service means developers provision within guardrails — not tickets, not root access. The guardrails (quotas, policies, defaults) are what make freedom safe.

Every self-service action needs: sensible defaults (secure by default), policy checks (OPA-style admission), and observability (who provisioned what, when). Freedom without these is anarchy with extra steps.
The ticket-queue trap: if the platform team hand-provisions, they become the bottleneck they were built to remove. Automate the top three requests first — they are usually 80% of tickets.
Backstage-style catalogs make self-service discoverable: services, templates, docs, and ownership in one place. Undiscoverable self-service is unused self-service.

example.code:
self-service request:
  kind: Database
  class: postgres-ha      # pre-approved classes only
  size: medium            # quota-checked
  owner: team-payments    # ownership required
  # policy engine verifies: class allowed, quota available,
  # backup enabled by default, network policy attached
example.walkthrough: The request shape is the design: constrained choices (classes, sizes) instead of free text. Constraints are what let you approve automatically — policy as code replaces the human approver.

pitfalls: Free-text self-service. Unconstrained input cannot be auto-approved.
Defaults that are insecure. Secure-by-default or every team misconfigures differently.
Skipping ownership. Unowned resources are un-deletable resources.
lessons.try_it: List your team's top five provisioning tickets; design the self-service request for number one.

lessons.title: Platform Engineering — Standards That Stick
concepts: Standards stick when they are the default, not the rule: the template ships with the standard built in, so compliance is automatic and deviation takes effort. Defaults beat mandates.
Version standards like code: base-image v2.1.0, pipeline template v3. The version lets you roll out changes (new TLS minimum) and measure adoption per version.
Exceptions need a process, not a fight: a lightweight exemption with expiry and review. No-exception standards get bypassed secretly; expiring exceptions stay visible.
Measure adoption, not compliance theater: percentage of services on current template version, not 'did everyone sign the policy.' Metrics drive the migration; mandates drive resentment.

example.code:
Standard rollout:
  v2.2.0: base image bumps OpenSSL (CVE fix)
  week 1: template updated, pilot teams green
  week 2: broadcast + self-service upgrade PR bot
  week 4: 80% adoption -> remaining get help, not blame
  week 6: exemptions expire; stragglers get pairing time
example.walkthrough: The rollout reads like a product launch because it is one: communicate the why, make upgrading one click, help the stragglers. Standards are adopted, not imposed.

pitfalls: Mandate without migration path. 'Upgrade by Friday' with no tooling is a morale event.
Permanent exceptions. Exemptions must expire or they become the standard.
Measuring signatures on policy docs. Measure template versions in production.
lessons.try_it: Pick one standard your org struggles with; design the default that would make it automatic.

lessons.title: Platform Engineering — Platform Economics
concepts: Platform work has a cost model: build cost (team time), adoption cost (migration, training), and the avoided cost (toil eliminated, incidents prevented). Fund it like an investment with measured returns.

Chargeback vs showback: chargeback (teams pay) drives accountability but creates accounting wars; showback (report costs, no charge) drives awareness without friction. Start with showback; the data earns the harder conversation.

The build-vs-buy line: undifferentiated heavy lifting (CI runners, artifact storage) is usually cheaper bought; your differentiation is the golden path glue. Build where you differ, buy where you do not.

Toil accounting: track hours the platform eliminates (manual deploys, ticket provisioning) and hours it creates (template maintenance). A platform that creates more toil than it kills is a cost center with good branding.

example.code:
Toil ledger (quarterly):
  ELIMINATED: 40h/wk manual deploys + 15h/wk ticket provisioning
  CREATED:   10h/wk template maintenance + 5h/wk platform on-call
  NET:       -40h/wk toil  ->  1 FTE freed for product work
  Report this number. It is the platform's P&L.
example.walkthrough: The toil ledger is how platforms survive budget season: it translates engineering virtue into capacity numbers finance understands. Without it, the platform is 'overhead.'

pitfalls: Ignoring adoption cost. A platform nobody migrates to has infinite cost per user.
Chargeback on day one. Meter first, argue about money later.
Building undifferentiated plumbing. Your CI runner is not a moat.
lessons.try_it: Estimate the toil your team spends weekly on manual provisioning and deploys; that is the platform's budget.

lessons.title: Platform Engineering — Failure Modes of Platforms
concepts: The ivory tower: platform built without developer input, optimizing for architectural purity. Symptom: 5% adoption and a shadow platform in every team.
The ticket-queue regression: self-service promised, manual fulfillment delivered. Symptom: platform team drowning, developers waiting — the old ops model with new branding.
The golden cage: one blessed path with no escape hatches. Symptom: advanced teams route around the platform entirely. Golden paths need paved exits for legitimate exceptions.
The resume-driven platform: exotic tech chosen for novelty, unmaintainable by the team that inherits it. Boring technology wins platform work — the platform must outlive its builders' enthusiasm.

example.code:
Failure-mode checklist (quarterly retro):
  [ ] Adoption: >50% of new services on golden path?
  [ ] Escape hatches: documented, used without shame?
  [ ] Toil trend: platform toil flat or falling?
  [ ] Bus factor: could the team maintain this if two people left?
  Any 'no' is a roadmap item, not a shame item.
example.walkthrough: Naming the failure modes in advance is the defense: teams that can say 'we're becoming a ticket queue' can correct. The checklist makes the drift visible before it is fatal.

pitfalls: Treating low adoption as a marketing problem. It is usually a product problem.
No escape hatches. The platform that forbids exceptions gets circumvented.
Novelty as strategy. The platform is infrastructure; infrastructure should be boring.
lessons.try_it: Score your platform (or last employer) against the four failure modes; pick the worst and propose one fix.

lessons.title: Platform Engineering — The Team Topologies View
concepts: Four team types: stream-aligned (product delivery), enabling (like platform teams — help others), complicated-subsystem, and platform (provide services). Platform teams are enabling by default; they succeed when stream teams ship faster.
Interaction modes: collaboration, X-as-a-service, facilitating. Platform teams should default to X-as-a-service (self-service APIs) and reserve collaboration for onboarding new capabilities.

Cognitive load is the constraint: a team can only hold so much. The platform's job is reducing the cognitive load of infrastructure on product teams — every leaked abstraction is load you failed to absorb.
Team APIs: the platform's interface (docs, CLIs, contracts) is as designed as its code. If using the platform requires reading its source, the team API is broken.

example.code:
Cognitive-load audit:
  PRODUCT TEAM must know: git push, pipeline status, dashboards
  PLATFORM ABSORBS: cluster upgrades, cert rotation, CVE patching,
                    capacity planning, backup verification
  LEAKED: teams hand-editing ingress annotations to fix TLS
  FIX: TLS termination as a platform default, not a per-team chore
example.walkthrough: The audit's question — 'what must product teams know that we could absorb?' — is the platform roadmap generator. Every leaked item is a feature request from reality.

pitfalls: Platform team owning product runtime. Enablement, not ownership — or you become the bottleneck.
Collaboration as default. It does not scale; X-as-a-service does.
Ignoring cognitive load. The platform that teaches everyone Kubernetes failed at abstraction.
lessons.try_it: Run the cognitive-load audit on one product team; list three items the platform should absorb.

lessons.title: Cluster Architecture: Control Plane and Nodes
concepts: The control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) is the brain: etcd holds the desired state, controllers converge reality to it. Lose etcd quorum and the cluster is brain-dead — workloads run, but nothing can change.
Nodes run kubelet (talks to the API), kube-proxy (service networking), and a container runtime. The kubelet is the node's agent: it ensures the pods assigned to it are running.
Managed control planes (GKE, EKS, AKS) remove the hardest operational burden — etcd — at the cost of control. For most platform teams, managed is the right call; self-host only with a reason.
HA design: 3+ control-plane nodes across zones, etcd on dedicated disks, API server behind a load balancer. Test control-plane failure — kill a member and watch quorum hold.

example.code:
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -o wide  # control plane static pods
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt endpoint health
example.walkthrough: etcd is the cluster's single source of truth and its most precious component: back it up, monitor its disk latency (slow disks = slow everything), and never let it share fate with workloads.

pitfalls: Single control-plane node in production. One failure from a very bad day.
etcd on shared slow disks. etcd latency is cluster latency.
Ignoring control-plane monitoring. The brain needs its own health checks.
lessons.try_it: Draw your cluster's control-plane topology; mark the quorum failure threshold.

lessons.title: Workloads: Deployments, StatefulSets, and Jobs
concepts: Deployments manage stateless replicas: declarative desired state, rolling updates, rollbacks via revision history. The workhorse for APIs and web services.
StatefulSets give stable identity: predictable pod names, ordered startup, persistent storage per pod. Databases, Kafka, ZooKeeper — anything where identity and storage matter.
Jobs and CronJobs run to completion: batch work, migrations, scheduled tasks. Set activeDeadlineSeconds and backoffLimit — a Job without bounds is a fork bomb with extra steps.
Choose by state: no state → Deployment; identity + storage → StatefulSet; run-to-completion → Job; scheduled → CronJob. The wrong controller is the root of half of all Kubernetes incidents.

example.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: api}
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: {maxUnavailable: 1, maxSurge: 1}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: registry/api:1.4.2   # never :latest
        readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /ready, port: 8080}}
example.walkthrough: maxUnavailable: 1 with 3 replicas means the rollout never drops below 2 serving pods — the arithmetic of safe rollouts. Probes are what make rolling updates safe: without readiness, the new pod gets traffic before it can serve.

pitfalls: image: :latest in production. Unreproducible deploys and surprise updates.
No probes. Rolling updates become rolling outages.
Stateful workloads in Deployments. Identity loss on reschedule corrupts data.
lessons.try_it: Convert one of your services' compose files to a Deployment with probes; explain each field.

lessons.title: Networking: CNI, Services, and Ingress
concepts: The CNI plugin gives every pod an IP and routes between them — the cluster's underlay. Calico, Cilium, Flannel: choose by policy needs (Calico/Cilium for NetworkPolicy enforcement).

Services are stable virtual IPs over ephemeral pods: ClusterIP (internal), NodePort, LoadBalancer (cloud LB per service — expensive), and headless (direct pod DNS for StatefulSets). kube-proxy programs the routing.
Ingress is L7 routing: one entry point, host/path rules to services. Ingress controllers (nginx, Traefik, gateway API) implement it. TLS terminates here — cert-manager automates issuance and renewal.
NetworkPolicy is the firewall: default-deny all ingress, then allow explicitly per workload. Without it, every pod can reach every pod — lateral movement's dream.

example.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: api-deny-all}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}}]
    ports: [{port: 8080}]   # only web -> api:8080
example.walkthrough: Default-deny plus explicit allow is the zero-trust posture for pod networking: start closed, open deliberately, and every rule documents an intended communication path. Audit the rules quarterly — they rot.

pitfalls: No NetworkPolicy. Flat network = blast radius of the whole cluster.
LoadBalancer per internal service. Cloud bill shock; use ClusterIP + Ingress.
Manual TLS certs. They expire at 3 AM; cert-manager does not sleep.
lessons.try_it: Apply a default-deny policy in a test namespace; watch what breaks and allow it explicitly.

lessons.title: Operators and CRDs: Extending the API
concepts: CRDs let you define new resource types (e.g., Database, Certificate); operators are controllers that reconcile them — the Kubernetes pattern applied to your domain: declare desired state, converge reality.
The operator pattern: watch custom resources, compare desired vs actual, act to close the gap, update status. It is the controller loop you already know, pointed at databases instead of pods.
When to build vs buy: databases, certs, and queues have mature operators — write one only for genuinely custom lifecycle logic. An operator is a long-term maintenance commitment.
cert-manager is the canonical example: declare a Certificate, it obtains and renews TLS certs, stores them as Secrets. Study it before building anything — it is the pattern done right.

example.code:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata: {name: api-tls}
spec:
  secretName: api-tls-secret
  issuerRef: {name: letsencrypt-prod, kind: ClusterIssuer}
  dnsNames: [api.example.com]
  # cert-manager obtains, renews, and stores the cert automatically
example.walkthrough: The Certificate resource shows the operator value proposition: a 10-line declaration replaces a runbook (generate CSR, prove domain, install cert, calendar reminder to renew). Every manual operational loop is an operator candidate.

pitfalls: Writing an operator for a solved problem. Check the ecosystem first.
CRDs without status subresources. Status is how users observe convergence — omit it and they are blind.
Operators that fight the platform. Reuse the controller patterns; do not reinvent leader election.
lessons.try_it: Install cert-manager on your kind cluster; issue a self-signed cert and watch the renewal logic.

lessons.title: Multi-Cluster Operations
concepts: Why multiple clusters: blast-radius isolation (prod vs dev), regulatory boundaries, and regional presence. One giant cluster is a single failure domain with extra steps.
Fleet management: GitOps per cluster (one repo or repo-per-cluster), cluster API for provisioning, and a management cluster pattern. Consistency across clusters comes from code, not from memory.

Service connectivity across clusters: multi-cluster Services, gateways, or service mesh (east-west gateways). Start with DNS + ingress per cluster; add mesh only when cross-cluster traffic needs policy.
Upgrades are the multi-cluster tax: version skew policy (n-2), upgrade dev first, then staging, then prod — with the GitOps repo as the version record. Never upgrade prod first.

example.code:
Fleet layout:
  mgmt-cluster: provisions workload clusters (Cluster API)
  fleet-infra repo: baseline per cluster (CNI, ingress, monitoring)
  workload repos: per-team, per-cluster overlays
  promotion: dev cluster -> staging -> prod (GitOps PRs)
  rule: clusters differ by config, never by hand
example.walkthrough: The fleet rule — clusters differ by config, never by hand — is what makes ten clusters operable by a small team. Every snowflake cluster is a future incident with a timezone.

pitfalls: One cluster for everything. Dev experiments share fate with prod revenue.
Hand-built clusters. If cluster #4 differs from #3, you have four pets.
Cross-cluster mesh on day one. Solve it with DNS until policy demands more.
lessons.try_it: Design the fleet layout for a company with dev/stage/prod across two regions; name the repos.

lessons.title: Pipeline Anatomy: Stages and Gates
concepts: A pipeline is a staged automation: source → build → test → scan → artifact → deploy. Each stage is a gate: failure stops the line. A pipeline without gates is a script with branding.

CI (continuous integration): every commit builds and tests — fast feedback on small batches. CD splits: continuous delivery (artifact always releasable, human promotes) vs continuous deployment (every green main goes to prod).
Pipeline as code: the pipeline definition lives in the repo, versioned and reviewed like application code. Click-ops pipelines are unreviewable, unrepeatable pets.
Speed budget: the inner loop (commit → signal) should be under 10 minutes. Slow pipelines train developers to batch big risky commits — the opposite of CI. Parallelize, cache, and split test suites.

example.code:
stages:
  - lint        # 1 min, fail fast
  - unit-test   # 3 min, parallel shards
  - build       # docker build, layer cache
  - scan        # vuln + secrets, blocks on critical
  - push        # immutable tag to registry
  - deploy-dev  # auto; stage/prod are promotions
example.walkthrough: The stage order encodes economics: cheap fast checks first (lint), expensive slow ones later (e2e). Fail fast is not impatience — it is respecting the developer's attention as the scarcest resource.

pitfalls: One giant stage. No gates, no signal about what failed.
Flaky e2e blocking every commit. Quarantine flakes or developers route around CI.
30-minute pipelines. Developers will batch, and batching is risk.
lessons.try_it: Time your team's commit-to-signal; list the three slowest stages and one fix each.

lessons.title: Artifacts and Registries
concepts: Build once, promote everywhere: the artifact (container image) is built a single time and promoted through environments by reference. Rebuilding per environment reintroduces variance — the thing CI was built to kill.
Immutable tags: every build gets a unique immutable tag (git SHA, semver). :latest and branch tags are mutable pointers — unreproducible and un-auditable.
Registries are infrastructure: Harbor, ECR, GAR — with retention policies, replication, and vulnerability scanning. An image you cannot pull at 3 AM does not exist.
SBOMs (software bills of materials) and signatures (cosign): know what is in the image and prove who built it. Supply-chain security starts at artifact creation.

example.code:
docker build -t registry/api:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) .
cosign sign --key cosign.key registry/api:<sha>
syft registry/api:<sha> -o spdx-json > sbom.json
# promote: same digest dev -> stage -> prod, never rebuilt
example.walkthrough: The digest is the identity: promoting by digest (not tag) guarantees stage and prod run bit-identical artifacts. Tags are human conveniences; digests are the truth.

pitfalls: Rebuilding per environment. 'Works on stage' means nothing if prod got a different build.
Mutable tags in prod. Rollback becomes archaeology.
No retention policy. The registry fills, pulls fail, 3 AM pages follow.
lessons.try_it: Trace one production image back to its commit, SBOM, and signature; note every gap.

lessons.title: Testing Gates: The Pyramid in Practice
concepts: The test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, few slow e2e tests. Invert it (e2e-heavy) and the pipeline becomes slow, flaky, and ignored.
Contract tests for services: consumer-driven contracts verify API compatibility without spinning up the world. They catch the breaking change that unit tests miss and e2e finds too late.
Flaky-test discipline: quarantine flakes immediately (separate suite, owner, deadline), never let them block the line. A flaky gate teaches developers that red is normal — then real red is ignored.
Coverage as signal, not target: 80% with meaningful assertions beats 95% of assertTrue(true). Mutation testing measures test quality; coverage measures test quantity.

example.code:
Gate layout:
  PR: lint + unit (fast, blocking)
  merge to main: integration + contract (blocking)
  nightly: full e2e + performance (informational, then promoted)
  release: smoke tests post-deploy (blocking promotion)
  Rule: blocking gates must be fast AND reliable.
example.walkthrough: The layout's principle: blocking power must be earned by speed and reliability. A slow or flaky gate blocking merges is a tax developers will evade — move it to nightly and keep the line green.

pitfalls: Blocking on flaky e2e. Red-normal pipelines are worse than no gates.
Coverage targets without assertion quality. 100% coverage, 0% confidence.
No contract tests between services. Integration surprises arrive in production.
lessons.try_it: Identify your pipeline's flakiest gate; propose quarantine or fix with an owner and date.

lessons.title: Progressive Delivery: Beyond Big-Bang Deploys
concepts: Progressive delivery releases in stages with automated judgment: canary (small % traffic, compare metrics), blue-green (two environments, instant switch), feature flags (decouple deploy from release).
Canary analysis: route 5% to the new version, compare error rate/latency against baseline, auto-promote or auto-rollback. The metrics decide — not hope, not the loudest engineer.
Feature flags separate deployment (code is live) from release (users see it): flags enable gradual rollouts, instant kill-switches, and trunk-based development without long-lived branches.
Database migrations are the hard part: expand-then-contract (add column, dual-write, migrate, remove old) keeps every deploy reversible. A deploy you cannot roll back is a leap of faith.

example.code:
canary:
  steps:
    - setWeight: 5
    - pause: {duration: 10m}
    - analysis:
        metrics:
          - name: error-rate
            successCondition: result < 0.01
    - setWeight: 50
    - analysis: {metrics: [error-rate, p99-latency]}
    - setWeight: 100
example.walkthrough: The analysis step is the innovation: the rollout watches the same SLOs you page on, and halts itself. This turns deploys from ceremonies into experiments with automatic safety.

pitfalls: Big-bang deploys of risky changes. The blast radius is 100% by choice.
Feature flags without cleanup. Stale flags are tech debt with runtime behavior.
Irreversible migrations. If down is impossible, up had better be perfect.
lessons.try_it: Design the canary analysis for your riskiest service: metrics, thresholds, and rollback trigger.

lessons.title: Pipeline Security: Protecting the Factory
concepts: The pipeline is production infrastructure: it holds deploy credentials, signs artifacts, and touches every environment. Compromise the pipeline and you compromise everything it ships.
Least-privilege pipeline identity: OIDC federation (no long-lived cloud keys in CI), per-environment roles, short-lived tokens. A leaked CI secret should expire before it is useful.
Protect the definition: pipeline-as-code with required reviews, branch protection, and pinned action versions (SHA, not @v4). A malicious PR that edits the pipeline is a supply-chain attack.

Artifact verification at deploy: admit only signed images from trusted builders (admission controllers checking cosign signatures). The cluster should distrust everything the pipeline did not vouch for.

example.code:
# GitHub Actions: OIDC instead of stored keys
permissions:
  id-token: write   # mint OIDC token
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4  # via OIDC role
        with: {role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123:role/ci-deploy}
example.walkthrough: OIDC federation removes the secret entirely: the CI system proves its identity to the cloud, which mints short-lived credentials. Nothing to leak, nothing to rotate — the best secret is the one that never existed.

pitfalls: Long-lived cloud keys in CI secrets. They leak via logs, forks, and exfiltration.
Unpinned third-party actions. @v4 today, compromised tomorrow — pin SHAs.
Unsigned artifacts admitted to prod. The cluster cannot distinguish your build from an attacker's.
lessons.try_it: Audit one pipeline: list every secret it holds and replace each with OIDC or a short-lived alternative.

lessons.title: Terraform Core: Resources and Graphs
concepts: Terraform declares resources; the provider API creates them. terraform plan shows the diff (desired vs actual), apply converges. Plan-before-apply is the change-management ritual — never skip it in prod.

The dependency graph: Terraform builds resources in dependency order from references (subnet_id = aws_subnet.main.id). Implicit dependencies via references; explicit via depends_on for hidden ordering.
Providers are plugins (AWS, Kubernetes, Cloudflare); the registry versions them — pin provider versions or a registry update changes your plan under you.
terraform plan is a code review artifact: attach it to the PR. Reviewers approve the diff, not the HCL. No plan, no merge — the rule that prevents 3 AM surprises.

example.walkthrough: The plan output is the real interface: + / ~ / - tell you what will happen before it happens. Teams that review plans catch the accidental database replacement; teams that do not, restore from backup.

pitfalls: apply without plan in production. The plan is the review; skipping it is deploying blind.
Unpinned providers. A minor provider release can rewrite your diff.
Ignoring the ~ (update-in-place) vs -/+ (replace) distinction. Replacement destroys first.
lessons.try_it: Run plan on a test config; identify every +/~/- and predict the API calls.

lessons.title: State: Terraform's Memory
concepts: State maps declared resources to real ones (resource → cloud ID). Without state, Terraform cannot plan — it would not know what exists. State is the memory; the config is the intent.
Remote state backends (S3 + DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud, GCS): shared, locked, versioned. Local state files are single-player — the team that shares local state shares corruption.
State locking prevents concurrent applies from corrupting state. An apply that crashes mid-write without locking leaves half-recorded reality — the dreaded 'state says X, cloud says Y.'
State surgery (import, mv, rm) reconciles drift between state and reality — but every surgery is a risk. Prefer converging reality to config; operate on state only when the map itself is wrong.

example.code:
terraform init -backend-config=backend.hcl
terraform plan -out=tfplan      # save the reviewed plan
terraform apply tfplan            # apply exactly what was reviewed
terraform state list              # what terraform thinks exists
example.walkthrough: The plan-file workflow (plan -out, apply the file) closes the review gap: what was approved is what runs. Applying without the saved plan lets reality change between review and apply.

pitfalls: Local state on a laptop. Bus factor 1, no locking, no backup.
Manual cloud-console edits (drift). State and reality diverge; the next apply surprises.
Deleting state to 'fix' things. You orphaned real resources — they still bill.
lessons.try_it: Simulate drift: change a tag in the console, run plan, and read the diff that detects it.

lessons.title: Modules: Packaging Infrastructure
concepts: Modules package reusable infrastructure (a VPC module, a database module) with inputs (variables) and outputs. DRY for infrastructure — but premature abstraction is worse than duplication.
Module versioning: pin module sources to versions (git tags, registry versions). Unpinned modules update under you — the same lesson as providers, one level up.
The module granularity rule: extract a module at the third copy, not the first. Two similar VPCs are coincidence; three are a pattern. Early modules ossify the wrong abstraction.
Composition over inheritance: small focused modules (network, database) composed in a root module beat mega-modules with 40 variables. If the variable list needs documentation to navigate, split it.

example.walkthrough: The version pin is the contract: v2.1.0 today behaves like v2.1.0 next year. Module registries (private or public) make versions discoverable — git-URL modules work but versioning is manual.

pitfalls: Mega-modules with dozens of variables. Composition beats configuration.
Unpinned module sources. Your infra changes when someone pushes to main.
Abstracting at the first duplication. Two is coincidence; three is a pattern.
lessons.try_it: Extract a repeated resource block into a module at your third copy; version it.

lessons.title: Drift Detection and Remediation
concepts: Drift: reality diverges from code (console edits, out-of-band scripts, cloud-provider mutations). Undetected drift makes the next apply a surprise — possibly a destructive one.
Detection: scheduled plan runs (drift detection pipelines) that alert on non-empty diffs without applying. The plan becomes a monitoring check — infrastructure's version of a failing test.
Remediation policy: auto-remediate (apply on schedule) for safe resources, alert-and-review for dangerous ones (databases, IAM). Auto-applying a database replacement at 3 AM is worse than the drift.
Prevention beats detection: IAM policies denying console edits on managed resources, SCPs blocking dangerous actions, and culture — the console is read-only for Terraform-managed infrastructure.

example.code:
# nightly drift check (CI job, no apply):
terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -out=/dev/null
# exit 0: clean | 1: error | 2: drift detected -> alert
# alert routes to the owning team with the diff attached
example.walkthrough: detailed-exitcode turns plan into a monitor: exit 2 means 'reality moved.' The alert with the diff attached is the whole workflow — detection, context, and owner in one notification.

pitfalls: Drift detection without ownership. An alert nobody owns is noise.
Auto-remediating databases. Some diffs must never auto-apply.
No prevention. Detecting drift you could have blocked is toil.
lessons.try_it: Set up a nightly plan-only job on one stack; route exit-2 alerts to the owning team.

lessons.title: Policy as Code: Guardrails for IaC
concepts: Policy as code (OPA/Rego, Sentinel, Checkov): machine-checkable rules evaluated against plans — 'no public S3 buckets,' 'all resources tagged,' 'no 0.0.0.0/0 ingress.' Prevention at plan time, not apology at audit time.
Shift-left the guardrail: policy checks run in CI on the plan, blocking the PR. Finding the violation in the PR is cheap; finding it in the auditor's report is expensive.
Policy exceptions: allowlist with expiry and owner, not silent bypasses. Every exception is tech debt with a deadline — track it like one.
Start with 5 policies, not 50: unencrypted storage, public exposure, missing tags, wildcard IAM, untagged cost centers. The Pareto of cloud misconfigurations is small and well-known.

example.code:
package terraform.policy
# Deny S3 buckets without encryption
deny[msg] {
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
  not rc.change.after.server_side_encryption_configuration
  msg := sprintf("S3 bucket %s lacks encryption", [rc.address])
}
example.walkthrough: The deny-rule shape is the pattern: match the resource type, check the missing property, emit a human-readable message with the address. Five such rules catch the misconfigurations behind most breach headlines.

pitfalls: 50 policies on day one. Developers route around the noise; start with the fatal five.
Policies without messages. 'Deny' with no explanation is a support ticket.
Permanent exceptions. Expiry or it becomes the standard.
lessons.try_it: Write one policy (no public S3) and wire it to fail a test PR; verify the message is actionable.

lessons.title: The Three Pillars: Metrics, Logs, Traces
concepts: Metrics are numbers over time (counters, gauges, histograms): cheap, aggregatable, alertable. 'How many errors per second?' is a metric question. Prometheus is the reference implementation.
Logs are discrete events with context: expensive, detailed, searchable. 'What exactly failed for user X?' is a log question. Structure them (JSON) or they are write-only.
Traces follow requests across services: spans with parent-child relationships show where latency lives in a distributed call. 'Why is checkout slow?' is a trace question.
Correlate by exemplar and ID: metrics spot the symptom, traces localize the service, logs explain the instance. One incident, three lenses — the investigation flows metric → trace → log.

example.code:
# error rate as a ratio (the SRE's favorite query):
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
/
rate(http_requests_total[5m])
# p99 latency:
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
example.walkthrough: Ratios, not absolutes: error rate (not error count) stays meaningful as traffic scales. Histograms (not averages) reveal the tail — averages hide the users who suffer most. These two habits separate SRE queries from vanity dashboards.

pitfalls: Alerting on absolute error counts. Traffic doubles, pages double — noise.
Unstructured logs. grep-able is not queryable; JSON is the minimum.
Averages for latency. The p99 is the user experience; the average is a lie.
lessons.try_it: For your service, write the three queries: error-rate ratio, p99 latency, and request rate.

lessons.title: SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets
concepts: SLI (indicator): what you measure (99.9% of requests succeed). SLO (objective): the target (99.9% over 30 days). SLA (agreement): the contract with consequences. Measure SLIs, set SLOs, sign SLAs rarely.
Choose SLIs users feel: availability (success ratio), latency (p99 under X), correctness, freshness. 'CPU under 80%' is not an SLI — users do not feel your CPU.

Error budgets: 100% - SLO = budget for failure (0.1% at 99.9%). Spend it on velocity (risky deploys) when full; freeze features and pay reliability when empty. The budget converts reliability into a business decision.

Burn-rate alerting: alert on how fast the budget burns (fast burn = page now; slow burn = ticket). Alerting on the budget instead of raw thresholds ends alert fatigue — pages mean 'we are spending reliability too fast.'

example.code:
Error-budget policy:
  SLO: 99.9% success over 30d -> budget: 43m downtime/month
  BUDGET > 50%: deploy freely, take risks
  BUDGET < 25%: feature freeze, reliability work only
  BUDGET EXHAUSTED: halt deploys, incident review, buy back budget
  The budget is the shared language of product and SRE.
example.walkthrough: The policy's genius: it replaces arguments ('is this deploy safe?') with arithmetic ('do we have budget?'). Product gets velocity when reliability is healthy; SRE gets leverage when it is not.

pitfalls: SLIs nobody feels (CPU, memory). Measure the user experience.
SLOs without consequences. An SLO nobody acts on is a dashboard decoration.
Alerting on symptoms, not burn. Pages should mean budget-burn, not blips.
lessons.try_it: Define one SLI/SLO for your service and compute its monthly error budget in minutes.

lessons.title: Alerting Discipline: Pages That Matter
concepts: Every alert needs: a runbook link, a severity with meaning (page = human action required NOW), and a threshold tied to user impact or error budget. Alerts without these are noise with a pager.

The page/ticket split: page on symptoms users feel (burn rate, total outage); ticket on causes and warnings (disk 70%, cert expiring). If it pages and nobody acts, it was a ticket wearing a page's clothes.
Alert fatigue is a reliability incident: fatigued humans miss real pages. Track alert volume per on-call; every alert must earn its page. Silence, tune, or delete — there is no fourth option.
Runbooks are the alert's other half: symptom, diagnosis steps, known fixes, escalation. An alert without a runbook pages a human to improvise at 3 AM — the most expensive compute available.

example.code:
alert: HighErrorBudgetBurn
  expr: error_budget_burn_rate > 14  # burns 30d budget in ~2d
  for: 15m
  labels: {severity: page}
  annotations:
