    runbook: https://runbooks/errors-burn
    summary: "Error budget burning 14x: {{ $labels.service }}"
    action: "Check deploys in last 1h; rollback candidate."
example.walkthrough: The annotation block is the design: summary (what), runbook (where), action (first step). The on-call should know the first move before opening the laptop. for: 15m suppresses blips — the alert fires on sustained burn, not spikes.

pitfalls: Paging on CPU/memory. Page on user impact or budget burn.
Alerts without runbooks. Improvisation at 3 AM is not a process.
No for: clause. Every blip pages; humans learn to ignore pages.
lessons.try_it: Audit your five noisiest alerts: page, ticket, tune, or delete each one.

lessons.title: Incident Response: The Discipline
concepts: Incident roles: commander (decides, coordinates), scribe (timeline), responders (work). The commander does not debug — a debugging commander is a missing commander.
The timeline is the artifact: every action timestamped in the incident channel. Memory lies; the timeline does not. Debugging from memory replays the confusion; debugging from the timeline sees it.
Communication cadence: updates every 15-30 minutes to stakeholders, even if 'still investigating.' Silence breeds escalation; regular updates buy focus time.

Mitigate first, root-cause later: stop the bleeding (rollback, shed load, failover), then investigate. The incident is not the classroom — restore service, then learn. Severity is measured in user impact, not technical interest.

example.code:
First 15 minutes:
  0:00 declare incident, assign commander + scribe
  0:02 open incident channel, start timeline
  0:05 assess: what is the user impact? severity?
  0:10 mitigate: rollback? failover? shed load?
  0:15 first stakeholder update (even if: 'mitigating')
  LATER: root cause, postmortem, action items
example.walkthrough: The checklist's order is the lesson: roles before debugging, mitigation before root cause, communication throughout. Incidents fail on coordination long before they fail on technology.

pitfalls: Commander debugging. The incident loses its coordinator.
Skipping the timeline. The postmortem becomes fiction.
Root-causing during the fire. Restore first; the classroom opens after.
lessons.try_it: Run a 30-minute tabletop: inject a fake outage, practice roles and timeline.

lessons.title: Postmortems: Learning Without Blame
concepts: Blameless does not mean causeless: the postmortem asks 'what allowed this?' not 'who did this?' — systems, not people, are the unit of analysis. Humans are the most reliable component; fix the system that set them up.

The five-whys (or fault-tree): drill past the proximate cause to the systemic one. 'Engineer ran the wrong command' → 'why was the command available?' → 'why no guardrail?' — stop at the fixable system, not at human error.
Action items are the product: each with an owner and a date, tracked like any work. A postmortem without action items is a storytelling session; action items without owners are wishes.
Publish postmortems internally (and externally when appropriate): the organization's learning compounds only if the lessons are searchable. The same incident twice is a process failure, not bad luck.

example.code:
Postmortem template:
  SUMMARY: what happened, user impact, duration
  TIMELINE: timestamped facts (from the scribe's log)
  ROOT CAUSE: the systemic cause (5 whys)
  WHAT WENT WELL / WHAT DIDN'T
  ACTION ITEMS: owner + date each (max 5, or none get done)
  LESSON: one paragraph for the org
example.walkthrough: The template's constraint — max 5 action items — is deliberate: ten action items means zero get done. Fewer, owned, dated items beat comprehensive wish lists. The lesson paragraph is what future-you searches for.

pitfalls: Blaming the human. The human is never the root cause; the system that allowed it is.
Action items without owners. Unowned work does not happen.
Private postmortems. Unsearchable lessons are unlearned lessons.
lessons.try_it: Write a postmortem for your last incident (or a tabletop) using the template; cap at 5 actions.

lessons.title: Golden Paths: Paved Roads, Not Mandates
concepts: A golden path is the blessed way to build, test, and ship — templates, pipelines, and defaults that make the right way the easy way. Paved roads, not walls: developers can leave the path, but the path is obviously best.
Design from the developer's first hour: scaffold → run locally → push → see it live. Every minute of friction in the first hour compounds into distrust of the whole platform.
One golden path per workload type (API, worker, frontend), not one path for everything. The path encodes the org's standards (security, observability) so teams inherit them by walking it.
Maintain the path like a product: versioned, tested, with a changelog. A rotting golden path is worse than none — it teaches developers the platform cannot be trusted.

example.code:
Golden-path checklist (API service):
  [ ] scaffold: one command, working service in 5 min
  [ ] local: docker-compose mirrors prod topology
  [ ] CI: lint/test/scan/build on every push
  [ ] deploy: merge to main -> staging auto, prod promotion
  [ ] observe: dashboards + alerts provisioned, not hand-built
  [ ] docs: runbook for the 3 known failure modes
example.walkthrough: The checklist is the path's definition of done: each item removes a decision the developer would otherwise make (and possibly make wrongly). The path's value is decisions pre-made correctly.

pitfalls: Mandating the path with no exits. Advanced teams will route around it — provide paved exits.
The path as documentation. Golden paths are runnable, not readable.
Untested templates. The path rots; trust follows.
lessons.try_it: Walk your golden path as a new hire would; time every step and fix the slowest.

lessons.title: Self-Service That Works
concepts: Self-service = developers provision in minutes without tickets, within guardrails. The guardrails (quotas, policies, approved classes) are what make it safe; the speed is what makes it used.
The request shape matters: constrained choices (size S/M/L, postgres-ha class) instead of free text. Constraints enable auto-approval — policy as code replaces the human gatekeeper.
Day-2 included: provisioning must bundle backups, monitoring, and runbooks. Self-service that provisions an unmonitored database is a future incident with a provisioning UI.
Discoverability: a catalog (Backstage-style) listing services, templates, and docs. The best self-service in the world fails if developers cannot find it.

example.code:
request: database
  class: postgres-ha     # approved classes only
  size: medium           # quota-checked against team budget
  owner: team-checkout   # ownership mandatory
  backup: true           # default, not optional
  # policy engine: class allowed? quota fits? network policy attached?
example.walkthrough: Every field is a decision pre-made: the class encodes HA topology, the backup default encodes the DR policy, ownership encodes accountability. The developer chooses; the platform decides the safe envelope.

pitfalls: Free-text provisioning. Unconstrained input cannot be auto-approved.
Provisioning without day-2. Unmonitored resources are incidents-in-waiting.
No ownership field. Unowned resources cannot be decommissioned.
lessons.try_it: Design the self-service request for your most-ticketed provisioning flow.

lessons.title: Documentation Developers Read
concepts: Docs are the platform's UI: quickstart (5 minutes to value), how-to guides (task-shaped), reference (exhaustive), and runbooks (failure-shaped). Four shapes, four jobs — one wiki page does none of them.
The quickstart is the conversion funnel: a new developer should ship something in under 15 minutes. Time it with a real new hire; every minute over is a bug in the docs.
Runbooks are failure-shaped docs: symptom → diagnosis → fix → escalation. Write them from real incidents, not imagination — imagined runbooks describe systems that do not exist.
Docs as code: versioned with the platform, tested in CI (do the commands still work?), owned like code. Rotting docs are worse than none — they teach developers to distrust all docs.

example.code:
Runbook shape:
  SYMPTOM: checkout p99 > 2s (alert: HighLatency)
  DIAGNOSE: 1) check canary status 2) trace slow spans
             3) compare with last deploy time
  FIX: rollback via GitOps revert (command included)
  ESCALATE: #payments-oncall if not resolved in 15m
  LAST VERIFIED: 2026-09-15 (CI checks the commands monthly)
example.walkthrough: The last-verified date is the innovation: docs rot silently, so CI must execute the commands periodically. A runbook whose commands fail is a liability, not an asset.

pitfalls: One wiki page for everything. Four doc shapes, four jobs.
Imagined runbooks. Write from incidents, not from architecture diagrams.
Untested docs. Commands rot; CI must verify them.
lessons.try_it: Pick your most-used doc; time a new hire following it and fix every stall.

lessons.title: Measuring Developer Experience
concepts: Measure outcomes, not activity: lead time (commit → prod), deployment frequency, change failure rate, time to restore (DORA) — plus time-to-first-deploy and toil hours. These are the platform's vital signs.
Developer surveys (quarterly, short): 'how easy is it to ship?' with room for text. Numbers show trends; text shows causes. The survey is user research, not a satisfaction contest.
Support-ticket analysis: categorize #platform-help by topic; the top categories are the roadmap. Every repeated question is a doc or automation that does not exist yet.
Report like a product: quarterly platform review with metrics, survey themes, and shipped improvements. Visibility earns budget; invisibility earns cuts.

example.code:
Platform scorecard (quarterly):
  DORA: lead time 2d->4h | freq 1/wk->daily | CFR 15%->5% | MTTR 2h->20m
  ONBOARDING: time-to-first-deploy 3d->2h
  TOIL: platform tickets 40/wk->8/wk
  SURVEY: 'shipping is easy' 3.1->4.2/5
  Top ticket themes -> next quarter's roadmap
example.walkthrough: The scorecard's power is the before/after: it proves the platform's value in the language of outcomes. 'We exist' is not a metric; 'lead time dropped 12x' is.

pitfalls: Vanity metrics (services onboarded). Activity is not value.
Annual 50-question surveys. Nobody finishes; nobody acts.
Metrics without action. Every red number needs an owner and a plan.
lessons.try_it: Build the scorecard for your platform (or last team); identify the reddest number.

lessons.title: Inner Loop: Local Development
concepts: The inner loop (edit → run → test locally) determines developer velocity more than any platform feature: a 10-second loop beats a 10-minute loop by 60x per hour of coding.
Dev-prod parity: local should mirror prod topology (same services, same config shape) via containers or dev clusters. 'Works on my machine' is a parity failure, not a developer failure.
Hot reload, live dashboards, and fast tests are inner-loop features: the platform team owns the local story too, not just the cluster. Neglect the laptop and developers route around everything else.
Remote dev environments (cloud workspaces) solve 'works on my machine' by standardizing the machine — at the cost of offline work and latency. Choose by team distribution, not fashion.

example.walkthrough: Parity is about shape, not scale: one API replica locally vs three in prod is fine; different service names or env var shapes are not. The compose file is a contract with the manifests.

pitfalls: 'Works on my machine' as a joke. It is a platform bug — fix the parity.
10-minute local test loops. Developers will stop testing.
Ignoring the laptop. The inner loop is where velocity lives.
lessons.try_it: Time your inner loop (edit to verified); halve the slowest step.

lessons.title: Landing Zones: The Foundation
concepts: A landing zone is the pre-configured cloud foundation: account structure, networking, identity, logging, and guardrails — the paved ground every workload builds on. No landing zone means every team invents (and misinvents) the basics.

Account strategy: separate accounts per environment and workload (blast-radius isolation, cost attribution, policy boundaries). One account for everything is a single failure domain with a billing console.

Baseline controls: centralized logging (all accounts → one audit trail), SSO identity, SCP/guardrail policies denying dangerous actions, and mandatory tagging. The baseline is non-negotiable; workloads customize above it.
Landing zone as code: the foundation itself is Terraform/pipeline-managed and versioned. A hand-built landing zone is a pet at the worst possible layer.

example.code:
Account layout:
  mgmt (billing, identity, audit logs)
  security (centralized logging, guardrails)
  network (shared VPCs, transit)
  prod-workload-a, prod-workload-b (isolated)
  dev / staging (cheaper, looser policies)
  sandbox (auto-nuked weekly, free experimentation)
example.walkthrough: The layout's logic is blast radius plus attribution: prod workloads cannot see each other's failures or bills, and the sandbox's auto-nuke makes experimentation safe. Every exception to the layout should require justification.

pitfalls: One account for everything. Blast radius, billing, and policy all collapse.
Hand-built foundation. The layer everything stands on must be code.
No sandbox. Experimentation happens in prod by default.
lessons.try_it: Sketch the account layout for a 50-person company; justify each boundary.

lessons.title: Cloud Networking: VPCs and Beyond
concepts: VPC fundamentals: private subnets (workloads, no public IPs), public subnets (load balancers only), NAT for outbound, route tables and NACLs. The shape is the security posture.

Connectivity patterns: VPC peering (simple, non-transitive), Transit Gateway (hub-and-spoke at scale), PrivateLink (service-to-service without internet). Choose by scale: peering for few, transit for many.
DNS is load-bearing: private hosted zones per VPC, resolver rules for hybrid. Half of all 'network issues' are DNS issues wearing a disguise — check DNS first, always.
Egress control: know what leaves your network (NAT gateway logs, egress filtering). Data exfiltration and surprise bills both exit through the NAT — monitor it like a border.

example.walkthrough: The three-tier subnet shape encodes the security model physically: each tier's route table IS its policy. When the shape is right, whole vulnerability classes become structurally impossible.

pitfalls: Workloads in public subnets. Every instance is one misconfig from the internet.
Databases with internet routes. The shape should make this impossible.
Peering meshes at scale. Non-transitive peering becomes unmanageable past ~10 VPCs.
lessons.try_it: Audit one VPC against the three-tier shape; list every violation and its fix.

lessons.title: IAM: Identity as the Perimeter
concepts: In cloud, identity is the perimeter: every API call is authenticated and authorized. The network is secondary. Design IAM first, not last.

Least privilege via roles, not users: workloads assume roles (IRSA in Kubernetes, instance profiles); humans federate via SSO with short sessions. Long-lived access keys are the exception that must justify itself.

Policy structure: identity policies (who can do what) plus resource policies and permission boundaries (what is allowed at most). SCPs at the org level deny whole action classes — the guardrail layer.
Access review cadence: unused roles, wildcards in production, privilege creep. IAM rots silently — quarterly reviews with actual removals, not rubber stamps.

example.walkthrough: The condition key is the advanced move: attribute-based access (team tags) scales where per-role policies do not. One policy serves fifty teams because the tag does the routing. Design for the org you'll be, not the team you are.

pitfalls: Wildcard actions on wildcard resources in prod. Admin-by-default is breach-by-default.
Long-lived keys for workloads. Roles and federation exist for this.
No access reviews. Privilege only accumulates; review is the garbage collector.
lessons.try_it: Find one wildcard policy in your environment; narrow it to the actual actions used (CloudTrail tells you).

lessons.title: Cost Management: FinOps Basics
concepts: Cost visibility first: tag everything (team, service, environment), allocate spend, and make it visible to owners. You cannot optimize what you cannot attribute — untagged spend is unmanageable spend.

The big three levers: rightsize (most instances are oversized — start from metrics), commitments (reserved/savings plans for steady state, 30-70% discounts), and lifecycle (delete unattached volumes, old snapshots, idle LBs).
Anomaly detection: budget alerts per team plus anomaly monitors. Surprise bills are incidents — page the owner like one. A $50k overnight spike deserves the same urgency as an outage.
Showback before chargeback: report costs to teams first (awareness without warfare). Chargeback comes when the data is trusted and the org is ready — usually quarters later.

example.code:
# find unattached EBS volumes (the classic waste):
aws ec2 describe-volumes \
  --filters Name=status,Values=available \
  --query 'Volumes[*].{ID:VolumeId,Size:Size,AZ:AvailabilityZone}'
# find old snapshots: sort by StartTime, check AMI associations
example.walkthrough: The unattached-volume query is FinOps in miniature: a mechanical check for a well-known waste pattern, runnable on a schedule, attributable to an owner. Most cloud waste is this boring — which is why it compounds unnoticed.

pitfalls: No tagging. Unattributable spend cannot be optimized or owned.
On-demand for steady state. Commitments exist for the predictable 70%.
Treating cost as finance's problem. Engineers choose the instance types; engineers own the bill.
lessons.try_it: Run the waste queries on one account; total the monthly savings and attribute each to an owner.

lessons.title: Multi-Cloud Strategy
concepts: The honest reasons: best-of-breed services, negotiating leverage, regulatory requirements, and acquisition reality. 'Avoiding lock-in' alone rarely justifies the cost — be honest about which reason is yours.

The cost is real: two IAM models, two networking models, two billing systems, and engineers who must know both. Multi-cloud multiplies cognitive load — the platform must absorb it or product teams drown.

Abstraction strategy: abstract at the workload layer (Kubernetes, Terraform) not at the service layer (a least-common-denominator database API). Portable workloads, native services — use each cloud's strengths where chosen.
Primary/secondary, not 50/50: one cloud is home (deep integration, commitments), the other is tactical (specific services, DR). Symmetric multi-cloud doubles everything for little benefit.

example.code:
Decision framework:
  1. NAME THE REASON (leverage? regulation? acquisition?)
  2. PRICE THE LOAD (2x IAM, networking, billing, on-call knowledge)
  3. DRAW THE LINE (workload-portable via K8s/Terraform;
     services native per cloud)
  4. PICK PRIMARY (commitments + depth go here)
  If step 1 is only 'lock-in fear', stop: the price exceeds the risk.
example.walkthrough: The framework forces the conversation most orgs skip: multi-cloud is bought with operational load, and the load is permanent. 'Avoiding lock-in' is often cheaper to address with portable architectures on one cloud.

pitfalls: Multi-cloud by default. The load is certain; the benefit is hypothetical.
Least-common-denominator abstractions. You get two clouds' weaknesses.
Symmetric 50/50. Double the everything, half the depth.
lessons.try_it: Run the framework on your org: name the reason, price the load, draw the line.

lessons.title: Supply-Chain Security
concepts: The supply chain is the attack surface: base images, dependencies, build tools, and registries. Compromise any link and the malware ships with your signature on it.

Pin and verify: pinned base images (digests), lockfiles for dependencies, pinned CI actions (SHAs). Every unpinned input is a future surprise — the supply chain is only as deterministic as its inputs.

Scan in the pipeline: vulnerability scanning (images, dependencies), secret scanning (no credentials in code), license checks. Scan on every build — the new CVE lands between releases, not during them.
Sign and attest: cosign signatures plus SLSA attestations (who built it, from what source, with what steps). Admission controllers verify before deploy — the cluster trusts only attested artifacts.

example.code:
# verify before you trust:
cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry/api:<digest>
syft registry/api:<digest> -o spdx-json | grype  # sbom -> vuln scan
# admission: only images with valid signature + attestation deploy
example.walkthrough: The verify-before-deploy loop closes the chain: build produces SBOM + signature, the registry stores them, admission checks them. An unsigned image is indistinguishable from an attacker's — the cluster must not run what it cannot verify.

pitfalls: Unpinned base images. 'Latest' upstream changes under you — possibly maliciously.
Scanning only at release. CVEs land daily; scan every build.
No admission control. The pipeline's promises are unenforced at the cluster.
lessons.try_it: Trace one prod image: base digest, SBOM, signature, admission check — document every gap.

lessons.title: Secrets Management
concepts: Secrets are not config: API keys, DB passwords, TLS keys need encryption at rest, audit logging, rotation, and least-privilege access. Env vars in plaintext are the most common leak vector.

The right stores: cloud KMS/secrets managers, Vault, or external-secrets operator syncing to Kubernetes Secrets (with encryption at rest enabled — etcd stores secrets base64, not encrypted, by default).
Rotation without restarts: versioned secrets, dual-credential support during rotation, automated rotation schedules. Manual rotation is the reason secrets never rotate.
Never in code, logs, or chat: secret scanning in pre-commit and CI, log redaction, and a revocation procedure everyone knows. The leak will happen; the response time is the metric.

example.code:
# external-secrets: secret lives in the manager, syncs to k8s
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata: {name: db-creds}
spec:
  secretStoreRef: {name: vault-backend, kind: ClusterSecretStore}
  target: {name: db-creds}   # k8s Secret (etcd encrypted at rest)
  data: [{secretKey: password, remoteRef: {key: prod/db/password}}]
example.walkthrough: ExternalSecrets keeps the manager as the source of truth: rotation happens there, the operator syncs, workloads reload. No human ever sees the value — which is the point. The k8s Secret is a cache, not a store.

pitfalls: Secrets in git. Even private repos leak; history never forgets.
etcd without encryption at rest. Secrets are base64 — readable to anyone with etcd access.
Manual rotation. It will not happen; automate or accept stasis.
lessons.try_it: Audit one service: where do its secrets live, who can read them, when do they rotate?

lessons.title: Zero Trust on the Platform
concepts: Zero trust: never trust, always verify — every request authenticated, authorized, and encrypted, regardless of network location. The cluster network is hostile by default; identity is the perimeter.

Workload identity: SPIFFE/SPIRE or cloud workload identity (IRSA) gives every workload a cryptographic identity. Service-to-service auth uses identity, not IP allowlists — IPs are spoofable, identities are not.

mTLS everywhere (service mesh or equivalent): encrypted in transit, mutually authenticated. The mesh also gives policy (authorization per call) and telemetry — security and observability from one layer.
Defense in depth, platform edition: NetworkPolicy (segmentation) + mTLS (identity) + admission control (what can deploy) + runtime policy (what can execute). No single layer is the security.

example.code:
Zero-trust layers:
  1. ADMISSION: only signed, scanned images deploy
  2. NETWORK: default-deny NetworkPolicy, explicit allows
  3. IDENTITY: workload identity (SPIFFE/IRSA), no IP trust
  4. TRANSPORT: mTLS, mutually authenticated
  5. RUNTIME: allowlisted syscalls/binaries, no privileged
  Breach one layer; the next contains it.
example.walkthrough: The layering is the strategy: each layer assumes the previous failed. An attacker with a pod still faces mTLS identity, still faces runtime policy — the breach is contained by construction, not by hope.

pitfalls: IP-based trust between services. IPs are addresses, not identities.
TLS termination without mTLS. Encryption without authentication is half the job.
One layer as 'the security.' Depth is the point; single layers fail.
lessons.try_it: Map your platform against the five layers; the thinnest layer is your roadmap.

lessons.title: Compliance as Code
concepts: Compliance is continuous, not annual: the controls (encryption, logging, access reviews) must hold every day, proven by automation — not by a pre-audit scramble. Audit season should be boring.

Controls as code: encryption policies (deny unencrypted), logging baselines (all API calls to central trail), access reviews (quarterly, with removals). Each control is a pipeline check or a scheduled job.
Evidence collection: the audit trail IS the evidence — versioned policy definitions, passing pipeline runs, review records. Auditors want proof of continuous operation, not screenshots.
Map controls to frameworks once (SOC 2, ISO 27001, CIS benchmarks), then automate the mapping. The framework is the vocabulary; the automation is the compliance.

example.code:
Control pipeline:
  POLICY (rego): deny unencrypted storage
  CHECK (CI): every plan evaluated
  EVIDENCE: passing runs logged, immutable
  REVIEW (quarterly): exceptions expiring, owners confirmed
  AUDIT: export the evidence bundle — no scramble
  The audit is a report, not a project.
example.walkthrough: The pipeline turns compliance from a periodic panic into a property of the system: every deploy proves the controls held. 'Were we compliant in March?' becomes a query, not an investigation.

pitfalls: Pre-audit scrambles. If compliance needs a project, it was not continuous.
Screenshot evidence. Prove continuous operation with logs, not pictures.
Controls without owners. Every control needs a human accountable for its operation.
lessons.try_it: Pick one control (encryption at rest); trace it from policy to evidence to audit export.

lessons.title: Runtime Protection
concepts: Admission is the gate, runtime is the guard: even verified images can misbehave (compromised dependency, exploited vulnerability). Runtime policy constrains what running containers may do.

The controls: no privileged containers, read-only root filesystems, dropped capabilities (drop ALL, add NET_BIND_SERVICE), seccomp profiles, and allowlisted syscalls. Each removes a privilege class the attacker would use.

Runtime detection: Falco/Tetragon watching for anomalous behavior (shell in a container that should never shell, unexpected network connections). Detection complements prevention — assume some attacks land.
Image hygiene at runtime: minimal base images (distroless/scratch where possible) shrink the attack surface. Every binary in the image is a tool for the attacker; ship only what the app needs.

example.code:
securityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: true
  runAsUser: 10001
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities: {drop: [ALL], add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]}
  seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}
example.walkthrough: The securityContext is the workload's seatbelt: non-root, read-only, no escalation, minimal capabilities. It costs nothing at runtime and removes entire exploit classes. There is no reason a web API needs root.

pitfalls: Privileged containers. Root with all capabilities is container escape waiting to happen.
Writable root filesystems. Malware needs somewhere to write.
No runtime detection. Prevention fails; detection is the backstop.
lessons.try_it: Apply the hardened securityContext to one workload; verify it still runs, then try to break out (in a lab).

lessons.title: GitOps Principles
concepts: Declarative: the entire system state is described declaratively (YAML, not scripts). Versioned: the desired state lives in git — every change is a commit with an author, a message, and a review.

Pulled: agents inside the cluster pull the desired state and converge — not CI pushing with kubectl. Pull beats push: the cluster needs no inbound credentials, and the agent is the reconciliation loop.
Continuously reconciled: the agent watches for drift (cluster vs git) and corrects it — self-healing infrastructure. Manual cluster edits get reverted, loudly.

The git history is the audit log: who changed what, when, why — and rollback is git revert. Change management, compliance evidence, and disaster recovery all fall out of the version control you already have.

example.code:
GitOps loop:
  1. Developer merges PR (desired state changes in git)
  2. Agent detects new commit (pull, not push)
  3. Agent diffs desired vs actual
  4. Agent applies changes, reports health
  5. Drift detected later -> agent reverts to git state
  The cluster converges to git. Always.
example.walkthrough: The pull model is the security insight: CI never holds cluster credentials, so a CI compromise cannot directly touch production. The agent inside the cluster is the only writer — a much smaller attack surface.

pitfalls: CI pushing kubectl to prod. Credentials in CI are the attack surface.
Git as backup, not source of truth. If the cluster is the truth, git is decoration.
No drift correction. Manual edits persist; the 'source of truth' is fiction.
lessons.try_it: Diagram the push-vs-pull credential flow; mark where cluster credentials live in each.

lessons.title: Agents: Argo CD and Flux Patterns
concepts: The agent pattern (Argo CD/Flux): a controller in the cluster watches git repos, compares with cluster state, and syncs. The UI/API shows sync status per app — the whole fleet's state at a glance.
Application as a unit: an Application resource binds a git path to a cluster (namespace). Promotion = changing the git ref or image tag in the repo — a PR, reviewed, audited.
Sync policies: auto-sync (dev: fast feedback) vs manual (prod: deliberate promotion). Sync waves order resources (CRDs before workloads). The policy encodes your risk appetite per environment.
Health assessment: the agent reports app health (degraded, progressing, healthy) from resource states. The GitOps dashboard becomes the deployment truth — not CI logs, not chat.

example.walkthrough: targetRevision is the promotion lever: a PR bumping v1.4.1 → v1.4.2 is the deploy, reviewed and audited. prune removes deleted resources; selfHeal reverts drift. The Application resource makes the deployment declarative too.

pitfalls: Auto-sync to prod. Dev gets auto; prod gets deliberate.
Monorepo without paths. One giant sync unit means one giant blast radius.
Ignoring sync waves. CRDs must exist before the resources that use them.
lessons.try_it: Install Argo CD (or Flux) on kind; deploy an app from git and watch a drift get self-healed.

lessons.title: Drift: Detection and Discipline
concepts: Drift is the git/cluster divergence: manual kubectl edits, controller mutations, cloud-provider changes. The agent detects it by continuous diffing — drift is visible, named, and attributable.
Self-heal policy: dev self-heals (fast correction, low risk); prod alerts on drift and heals on approval (or heals immediately for known-safe resources). The policy matches the environment's risk.

Legitimate drift exists: autoscalers change replica counts, controllers add finalizers. Exclude volatile fields from diffing (ignoreDifferences) — drift detection must not cry wolf on normal operation.

The discipline: no manual cluster writes, ever. Every emergency kubectl edit becomes a git commit within the hour — or the agent reverts it and the incident repeats. Git is the truth; the cluster is the cache.

example.code:
# ignore autoscaler-driven replica churn in diffs:
ignoreDifferences:
- group: apps
  kind: Deployment
  jsonPointers: [/spec/replicas]
# HPA owns replicas; git owns the rest. Diff what matters.
example.walkthrough: ignoreDifferences is the pragmatism: the diff should show human-meaningful divergence, not controller noise. Tune it per resource type — the goal is a drift alert that always means 'a human did something.'

pitfalls: Self-heal on prod without thought. Reverting a legitimate emergency fix re-creates the incident.
No ignoreDifferences. HPA churn pages the drift alert into irrelevance.
Emergency edits never committed. The agent reverts; the incident returns.
lessons.try_it: Cause drift on purpose (kubectl edit), watch detection, then commit-or-revert per policy.

lessons.title: Promotion Strategies
concepts: Environment-per-branch vs environment-per-directory: directories (envs/dev, envs/prod) in one repo keep history unified; repos-per-env isolate blast radius. Choose by team size: small → directories, large → repos.
Promotion as PR: to promote, open a PR changing the image tag/ref in the next environment's directory. Review, CI validation (policy checks, diff), merge — the deploy is a code review.
Image promotion vs git promotion: promote the immutable artifact (same digest) by updating the reference in git. Never rebuild between environments — the GitOps repo records exactly what runs where.
Automated promotion with gates: dev auto-promotes on CI green; staging promotes with tests; prod promotes manually with SLO checks. The gates encode trust per environment.

example.code:
Promotion flow (directories):
  git: envs/dev/api -> tag 1.4.2 (auto on CI green)
  PR:  envs/staging/api -> tag 1.4.2 (tests pass)
  PR:  envs/prod/api -> tag 1.4.2 (SLOs green, approval)
  Each step: same digest, reviewed diff, auditable history.
  Rollback: revert the promotion PR.
example.walkthrough: The flow's elegance: promotion is just reference updates, so the history shows exactly which artifact ran where and when. Debugging 'what changed in prod?' becomes git log — the fastest incident tool ever built.

pitfalls: Rebuilding per environment. The promoted artifact must be bit-identical.
Manual tag edits without PR. Unaudited deploys are incidents waiting for discovery.
Promoting untested artifacts. Gates per environment, or prod tests what dev skipped.
lessons.try_it: Design the promotion flow for three environments; name the gate at each step.

lessons.title: Disaster Recovery with GitOps
concepts: GitOps simplifies DR enormously: the cluster is disposable because its entire state is in git. New cluster + agent + same repos = same workloads. The backup that matters is the git repo (plus data).
The DR drill: provision a fresh cluster, point the agent at the repos, watch everything converge. Time it. The RTO you have not measured is a hope, not a plan.

Data is the exception: git holds config, not database contents. Backup/restore for stateful data (snapshots, Velero) is the separate, harder half of DR — config recovery without data recovery is an empty victory.
Repo resilience: the git hosting itself needs backup/availability (mirrors, multiple remotes). The source of truth must survive the disaster it is meant to recover from.

example.code:
# DR drill sketch:
# 1. fresh cluster (cluster-api / managed)
# 2. install agent, point at git repos
# 3. watch sync: kubectl get applications -w
# 4. restore data from snapshots (velero restore)
# 5. verify: smoke tests, SLOs green
# 6. record RTO; improve; repeat quarterly
example.walkthrough: The drill's output is a number: minutes from 'clusters gone' to 'serving traffic.' Every DR plan without a measured RTO is fiction. Quarterly drills keep the number honest — and keep the team practiced.

pitfalls: Backing up YAML, forgetting data. Config without data is an empty shell.
No measured RTO. Unmeasured recovery is a hope.
Single git hosting with no mirror. The truth must survive the disaster.
lessons.try_it: Run the DR drill on kind: wipe the cluster, reconverge from git, time it.

lessons.title: Error Budgets in Action
concepts: The budget as policy: ship velocity is throttled by budget remaining — full budget means risk freely, empty means freeze. The policy is agreed in calm times so it binds in stressed ones.
Budget accounting: burn rate per service, per team, visible on dashboards. Teams that cannot see their budget cannot manage it — transparency is the mechanism.

Spending the budget wisely: canary risky changes when budget is full (that is what it is for); save budget before big events (launches, holidays). The budget is a resource to manage, not just a limit.

Negotiating SLOs: the SLO is a business decision (how reliable must this be?) with a cost (engineering time). SRE's job is making the cost visible so the business chooses deliberately — not discovering the choice after the outage.

example.code:
Budget meeting (monthly):
  SERVICE: checkout | SLO 99.9% | budget remaining 62%
  DECISION: risky migration approved (budget funds it)
  SERVICE: search   | SLO 99.95% | budget remaining 8%
  DECISION: feature freeze; reliability sprint scheduled
  No arguments about 'safety' — the arithmetic decides.
example.walkthrough: The meeting's format is the practice: numbers in, decisions out. Without the budget, the same meeting is opinions vs opinions — and the loudest voice wins instead of the data.

pitfalls: Budgets nobody watches. Invisible budgets do not bind.
One SLO for everything. Critical paths deserve tighter SLOs than admin pages.
Budget as punishment. It is a planning tool, not a blame tool.
lessons.try_it: Compute one service's budget status; make the ship/freeze call explicitly.

lessons.title: Toil: Identify, Measure, Eliminate
concepts: Toil defined: manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, no enduring value, scaling with service growth. Ticket-provisioning, manual deploys, hand-run migrations — toil is the work that grows as you succeed.
The 50% rule (Google SRE): no more than half of SRE time on toil — the rest on engineering (automation, architecture). Past 50%, the team is ops with a fancy title, and toil grows unbounded.
Toil accounting: log toil hours by category weekly. What gets measured gets automated — the ledger turns complaints ('so many tickets') into projects ('automate provisioning: 15h/wk').
Eliminate, don't endure: every toil category gets either automation or elimination (is this ticket necessary at all?). Enduring toil is how platforms become ticket queues.

example.code:
Toil ledger (weekly):
  manual deploys:      12h  -> automate via pipeline (project)
  ticket provisioning: 8h  -> self-service portal (project)
  cert renewals:       3h  -> cert-manager (done)
  log diving for devs: 6h  -> self-service dashboards (project)
  TOTAL: 29h/wk toil  |  SRE capacity: 80h  |  toil ratio: 36%
example.walkthrough: The ledger's ratio is the headline: 36% is healthy, trending down. The project column is the roadmap — each row is toil with an expiration date. Toil without a project is permanent.

pitfalls: Calling all ops work toil. Engineering (automation, design) is not toil — it is the cure.
No measurement. Unmeasured toil is infinite toil.
Automating without eliminating. Sometimes the ticket should not exist at all.
lessons.try_it: Log your team's toil for one week; categorize and total it.

lessons.title: Capacity Planning
concepts: Capacity is a forecast, not a feeling: model growth (traffic trends), headroom (N+1 minimum — survive one failure), and events (launches, seasons). Plan quarterly; review monthly.
The utilization paradox: high utilization looks efficient until a spike or failure needs headroom. Target 60-70% steady-state for critical paths — the 'waste' is the insurance premium.

Autoscaling handles variance, not planning: HPA/VPA react to load, but they need configured bounds, tested scale-up speed, and quota headroom. An autoscaler that has never scaled is untested capacity.
Load test the plan: synthetic traffic at projected peak, watch where it breaks, fix the bottleneck, repeat. The bottleneck you find in the test is cheap; in production it is an incident.

example.code:
Capacity model:
  CURRENT: 1000 rps peak, 40% utilization (2500 rps capacity)
  GROWTH: 10%/quarter -> 1460 rps peak in 4 quarters
  HEADROOM: N+1 -> need 2x peak = 2920 rps
  PLAN: scale to 3000 rps capacity by Q3; load-test at 3000
  TRIGGER: replan if growth exceeds 15%/quarter
example.walkthrough: The model's value is the trigger: growth assumptions are written down, so exceeding them triggers replanning instead of surprise. Capacity planning is assumption management.

pitfalls: 100% utilization targets. Efficient until the first spike.
Untested autoscaling. Scale-up speed and quota limits are the gotchas.
No growth model. 'We'll scale when needed' is not a plan.
lessons.try_it: Build the capacity model for one service; name the trigger that forces replanning.

lessons.title: Chaos Engineering
concepts: Chaos engineering: hypothesis-driven failure injection — 'we believe the system survives zone loss because traffic shifts in 60s' — then test it. Science, not vandalism.
Start small, in prod-ish environments: kill pods, add latency, lose a zone. The blast radius starts tiny and grows with confidence — game days graduate to continuous chaos.

The hypothesis is the point: 'the checkout survives payment-service latency' is falsifiable; 'let's break things' is not engineering. Every experiment states the expected steady state and the abort conditions.
Findings become fixes: the experiment that reveals the missing timeout becomes a ticket, then a verification experiment. Chaos without follow-through is just breakage with extra steps.

example.code:
Experiment card:
  HYPOTHESIS: losing one AZ shifts traffic in <60s, p99 < 1s
  BLAST RADIUS: staging only, business hours, abort on SLO breach
  INJECT: blackhole AZ-b for 10 minutes
  MEASURE: traffic shift time, p99, error rate
  ABORT: error budget burn > 5x OR any data loss signal
  FOLLOW-UP: ticket for every deviation from hypothesis
example.walkthrough: The abort conditions are what make it engineering: the experiment stops itself before causing the incident it is meant to prevent. Chaos without abort criteria is just an outage you scheduled.

pitfalls: Chaos in prod on day one. Graduate the blast radius with confidence.
No hypothesis. Breaking things without a question is vandalism.
Experiments without follow-up. Findings that do not become tickets are theater.
lessons.try_it: Write one experiment card for your riskiest assumption; define the abort conditions.

lessons.title: Learning from Failure: Beyond Postmortems
concepts: Postmortems are the start: the learning organization also does pre-mortems ('imagine this failed — why?'), game days (practice the failure), and failure libraries (searchable incident history).
Pre-mortems beat postmortems on cost: an hour imagining failure modes before launch finds the missing runbook, the untested rollback, the unclear ownership — all fixable before users are involved.
Track repeat incidents: the same failure twice is a process failure. Tag incidents by cause category; the recurring category is the systemic fix the org keeps avoiding.
Share externally when possible: public postmortems (with sensitive details removed) build industry trust and force clarity — writing for the public exposes hand-waving that internal docs tolerate.

example.code:
Pre-mortem (1 hour, before launch):
  'It's 3 months later. The launch failed badly.'
  Each person writes 3 reasons why. Share, cluster, vote.
  Top 3 reasons -> mitigations BEFORE launch.
  Cost: 1 hour. Value: the incident that never happened.
example.walkthrough: The pre-mortem's trick is prospective hindsight: imagining failure as fact unlocks candor that 'what could go wrong?' does not. People who will not voice doubts will write them when the failure is assumed.

pitfalls: Postmortem theater: documents nobody reads, actions nobody owns.
No repeat tracking. The third identical incident is organizational amnesia.
Blameful culture. Hidden failures do not become lessons.
lessons.try_it: Run a pre-mortem on your next launch; compare its findings with the actual launch issues.

lessons.title: The System Design Interview
concepts: The format: open-ended design ('design a CI/CD platform') in 45 minutes. They assess structured thinking, trade-offs, and depth — not the 'right' answer.

The method: clarify requirements (scale, users, constraints) → sketch high-level → deep-dive one component → discuss trade-offs and failure modes. Narrate your thinking; silence is the only wrong answer.
Drive with questions: 'How many deploys per day? What's the blast radius tolerance?' — requirements you assume are requirements you get wrong. Interviewers reward the asking.
Always end with failure modes and monitoring: 'what breaks, how do we know, how do we recover?' — the SRE instinct is what separates senior answers from architecture diagrams.

example.code:
45-minute structure:
  0:00-0:10  clarify: scale, users, constraints, non-goals
  0:10-0:25  high-level: components, data flow, key APIs
  0:25-0:38  deep dive: one hard component (e.g., the scheduler)
  0:38-0:45  trade-offs, failure modes, monitoring, scaling
  Narrate throughout. Ask before assuming.
example.walkthrough: The structure's discipline is time-boxing: candidates who spend 30 minutes on the high-level never reach the deep dive where seniority is judged. The deep dive is the interview; everything before is setup.

pitfalls: Jumping to tech choices. Requirements first — always.
Silent diagramming. Narrate; the thinking is the product.
No failure modes. 'What breaks?' is the senior question.
lessons.try_it: Practice: design a URL shortener in 45 minutes, recorded; review the time-boxing.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Interviews: Think Aloud
concepts: The format: a broken system, you diagnose live. They assess method: hypothesis → test → observe → refine. Random command-spraying fails; structured elimination passes.
The method: restate the symptom, list hypotheses by probability, test the cheapest first, narrate each step. 'Latency tripled after deploy' → check deploy diff first (base rates), not the kernel.
Use the pillars in order: metrics (what changed?), traces (where?), logs (why?). Say the order aloud — it shows you have a system, not just commands.
When stuck, say so and widen: 'my hypotheses are exhausted; let me check the assumptions — DNS, certs, quotas.' Naming the stuck point is strength; silent flailing is the fail mode.

example.code:
Live-debug script:
  1. SYMPTOM: 'checkout p99 3x since 14:00' (restate it)
  2. HYPOTHESES: deploy at 13:55 (likely), traffic spike, downstream slow
  3. CHEAPEST TEST: deploy diff + canary metrics (2 min)
  4. OBSERVE: canary errors up -> rollback candidate
  5. NARRATE: 'rolling back the correlated change first, then root-causing'
  Method beats knowledge; narrate the method.
example.walkthrough: The script's order encodes base rates: recent changes cause most incidents, so check them first. Interviewers watch whether your first move matches the probabilities — it reveals operational maturity.

pitfalls: Command spraying without hypotheses. Activity is not diagnosis.
Silent debugging. They cannot grade thinking they cannot hear.
Never checking assumptions. DNS, certs, quotas: the embarrassing classics.
lessons.try_it: Practice: break a kind cluster (bad probe, full disk) and debug aloud, recorded.

lessons.title: Behavioral Rounds: STAR with Systems
concepts: The format: 'tell me about a time...' — they assess ownership, conflict, and learning. Platform stories need the system's context: scale, stakes, and your specific leverage.

STAR with systems: Situation (the system and stakes), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — not the team), Result (measured: latency, incidents, toil hours). Numbers are the difference between a story and an anecdote.
Prepare six stories: outage you mitigated, disagreement you navigated, toil you eliminated, incident you learned from, platform you shipped, mistake you owned. Six stories cover 90% of questions.
The mistake story is the most important: own it fully, show the systemic fix, name what you do differently. Defensiveness fails; owned failure with a fix passes.

example.code:
STAR example (toil):
  S: 40h/wk manual deploys across 12 teams; deploys took 2 weeks
  T: I owned deploy automation as platform engineer
  A: built pipeline templates + self-service promotion; migrated 3 pilot teams
  R: lead time 2wk->4h; toil 40h->6h/wk; adopted org-wide in 2 quarters
  Numbers make it checkable; checkable is credible.
example.walkthrough: The numbers are the credibility mechanism: 'improved deploys' is a claim, '2 weeks to 4 hours' is evidence. Prepare the numbers before the interview — reconstructing them live is where stories die.

pitfalls: 'We' for everything. They are hiring you; name your leverage.
No numbers. Anecdotes without metrics are unverifiable.
Blaming others in the mistake story. Own it or fail it.
lessons.try_it: Write six STAR stories with numbers; rehearse each in under 3 minutes.

lessons.title: The Platform Portfolio: Show, Don't Tell
concepts: The capstone demo is the portfolio: a 15-minute recording of scaffold → CI → GitOps → break → alert → rollback. It proves run knowledge in a way resumes cannot.
Supplement with artifacts: architecture diagrams, runbooks, postmortems (sanitized), pipeline definitions. Each artifact answers 'show me' before it is asked.
Write about it: one blog post per hard problem (the canary that caught a bug, the toil you killed). Writing proves communication — the skill platform roles screen hardest for.
Keep it current: the portfolio rots like templates. Quarterly: re-record the demo, update the numbers, prune dead artifacts. A stale portfolio signals a stale engineer.

example.code:
Portfolio checklist:
  [ ] 15-min demo recording (build-ship-break-recover)
  [ ] architecture diagram (current)
  [ ] 2 sanitized postmortems showing learning
  [ ] pipeline + GitOps repo excerpts
  [ ] 1 blog post on a hard problem
  [ ] metrics: lead time, reliability, toil (before/after)
example.walkthrough: The checklist's principle: every claim on the resume gets an artifact. 'Built a platform' → the demo. 'Reduced toil' → the numbers. Interviewers probe claims; artifacts end probes.

pitfalls: Resume claims without artifacts. Every claim will be probed.
Stale demo from two years ago. Currency signals currency.
No writing. Communication is the screened skill; prove it in prose.
lessons.try_it: Record the 15-minute demo this week; get one peer review before publishing.

lessons.title: Your 8-Week Study Plan
concepts: Weeks 1-2: foundations — Kubernetes (labs!), Linux/networking refresh, one terminal proof per concept. No skipping labs; run knowledge starts here.
Weeks 3-4: delivery — CI/CD pipelines, IaC, GitOps. Build the capstone's phase 1-2 as you learn; the project is the practice.
Weeks 5-6: operations — observability, SRE practices, security. Run the incident tabletop; write the postmortem; do the chaos game day.
Weeks 7-8: integration — finish the capstone, take the mock twice, drill system design aloud, rehearse STAR stories. The last two weeks are performance, not learning.

example.code:
Weekly cadence:
  3x 90-min deep sessions (lesson -> scenarios -> lab)
  1x incident-ledger review (revisit every miss)
  1x capstone build session (the artifact grows weekly)
  Week 4: mock #1 (diagnostic) | Week 8: mock #2 (dress rehearsal)
  Daily: 15-min flash review of the ledger
example.walkthrough: The cadence's insight: the capstone grows alongside the curriculum, so week 8 has an artifact, not a cram session. The mocks bracket the plan — diagnostic early, rehearsal late.

pitfalls: Cramming in week 8. Performance needs rehearsal, not new content.
Skipping the ledger review. Unrevisited misses are unlearned lessons.
No mock until 'ready.' Readiness follows measurement.
lessons.try_it: Block the 8 weeks on your calendar now; schedule mock #1 for week 4.

labs.title: Catalog Your First Service
labs.objective: Register a service in a Backstage-style software catalog with ownership and lifecycle metadata.
steps: Write a `catalog-info.yaml` (Component kind) with name, description, lifecycle (`production`), and owner.
Define the owner as a `Group` entity (team name, members) referenced by the component.
Add annotations: repo URL, runbook link, and techdocs ref.
Validate the YAML structure (required fields: apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec).
Register it in the catalog UI/API and search for it by owner — confirm ownership is queryable.

checks.hint: The file should declare a Component entity.
Ownership must be present in the metadata or spec.

labs.title: Ship a Golden-Path Template
labs.objective: Build one parameterized software template that scaffolds a production-ready service skeleton.
steps: Define template parameters: service name, language (node/python), and workload type (api/worker).
Write the skeleton: Dockerfile (multi-stage, non-root), k8s manifests with probes and resource requests, CI pipeline stub.
Add template metadata: title, description, owner, and tags for catalog discoverability.
Scaffold two different services from the same template and diff the outputs — only parameters should differ.
Write a deprecation note for one legacy template this new one replaces.

checks.hint: The scaffolded output should include a Dockerfile.
The template definition should declare its parameters.

labs.title: Break and Fix the Probe
labs.objective: Deploy an app with a bad liveness probe, diagnose the CrashLoop, and fix it — the full failure loop.
steps: Deploy nginx with a liveness probe hitting /wrong-path and initialDelaySeconds: 2.
Watch it CrashLoop: kubectl get pods -w; note the restart count climbing.
Diagnose: kubectl describe pod — find the probe failure events; confirm the app itself is fine (curl via port-forward).
Fix the probe path and delay; watch the pod go Running with restarts reset.
Bonus: break the readiness probe instead — observe pods removed from endpoints WITHOUT restarts.

labs.title: Default-Deny NetworkPolicy
labs.objective: Lock down a namespace with default-deny and open only intended paths.
steps: Create namespace demo-net; deploy a frontend, api, and database pod.
Apply a default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy selecting all pods; verify frontend cannot reach api (curl fails).
Add an allow rule: frontend -> api:8080 only; verify it works and api -> frontend still fails.
Add db rule: api -> db:5432 only; verify frontend cannot reach db directly.
Document each rule as an intended communication path; note what an audit would ask.

labs.title: Build a Gated Pipeline
labs.objective: Create a minimal pipeline with real gates: lint, test, scan, and a blocking policy.
steps: Scaffold a tiny app repo with a Dockerfile and a test suite (one passing, one failing test).
Write a pipeline definition (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Tekton) with stages: lint -> test -> build -> scan.
Make the scan stage fail the pipeline on a planted critical CVE (use an old base image deliberately).
Fix by bumping the base image; watch the pipeline go green end to end.
Add branch protection requiring the pipeline: prove a direct push to main is rejected.

labs.title: Canary with Automatic Halt
labs.objective: Deploy a canary that watches error metrics and halts itself on regression.
steps: Deploy v1 of a demo app with a /metrics endpoint exposing error counts.
Configure a canary (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, or a manual weight script) at 10% traffic.
Deploy v2 with an injected 20% error rate; watch the analysis detect it and halt/roll back.
Verify: v1 serves 100% again with no manual intervention during the halt.
Write the runbook entry: 'canary halted' — what does the on-call do next?

labs.title: Plan-Driven Change with Drift Detection
labs.objective: Make a change through the full plan-review-apply cycle, then detect simulated drift.
steps: Write a Terraform config for a test resource (local_file, or a cloud test resource in a sandbox).
Run plan -out=tfplan; read every +/~/- and write what you expect to happen.
Apply the saved plan; verify reality matches.
Simulate drift: modify the resource out-of-band; run plan -detailed-exitcode and confirm exit 2.
Write the remediation: which diffs auto-remediate, which need review?

labs.title: Write and Enforce a Policy
labs.objective: Author an OPA/Checkov policy and wire it to block a violating plan.
steps: Write a Rego (or Checkov YAML) policy denying unencrypted storage resources.
Create a test Terraform plan JSON (terraform show -json tfplan) that violates it.
Run the policy evaluation; confirm it denies with a human-readable message naming the resource.
Fix the config, re-run, confirm it passes.
Document the exception process: who approves, how long it lasts, where it is tracked.

labs.title: Burn-Rate Alerting from Scratch
labs.objective: Instrument a demo app and build a burn-rate alert that pages on budget consumption.
steps: Deploy a demo app exposing RED metrics (use a sample or instrument a tiny Flask app with prometheus_client).
Define the SLI (success ratio) and SLO (99.9% over 30d); compute the error budget.
Write a burn-rate alert (14x fast-burn) with runbook annotation and a first-action step.
Inject errors to trigger it; verify the alert fires and the runbook's first step is correct.
Tune: adjust the for: clause until blips don't page but sustained burn does.

labs.title: Incident Tabletop Drill
labs.objective: Run a simulated incident with roles, timeline, and a blameless postmortem.
steps: Assign roles: commander, scribe, two responders. Inject a failure (kill a service, break a probe).
Run 30 minutes: commander coordinates only, scribe keeps the timestamped timeline, responders mitigate.
Mitigate (rollback/failover), then hold the postmortem: timeline review, five whys, max 5 action items.
Write the postmortem doc; each action item gets an owner and a date.
Retro the drill itself: where did role discipline break? Fix it next time.

labs.title: Time the Golden Path
labs.objective: Walk the new-hire path end to end, timing every step, and fix the slowest.
steps: Scaffold a service from your template as a new hire would (fresh clone, no tribal knowledge).
Time each step: scaffold, local run, first push, CI green, staging live, docs found.
Identify the slowest step and the step where you needed to ask a human.
Fix one: automate the stall, document the question, or simplify the step.
Re-time. Record before/after: this is your platform's onboarding metric.

labs.title: Ticket Archaeology
labs.objective: Mine the support channel for the roadmap: categorize, count, and convert top themes into fixes.
steps: Export one month of #platform-help (or ticket queue); categorize each thread (provisioning, deploys, docs, access, other).
Count by category; the top two are your next quarter's roadmap candidates.
For the top category, design the fix: self-service automation, doc shape, or guardrail.
Estimate the toil: threads × median resolution time = hours the fix would reclaim.
Present the one-slide case: problem, toil cost, proposed fix, expected reclaim.

labs.title: Subnet Discipline Audit
labs.objective: Audit a VPC against the three-tier shape and fix every violation.
steps: Map the VPC: list subnets, route tables, and what runs in each.
Classify each subnet: public (ALB only?), private (workloads?), data (no internet route?).
Flag violations: workloads with public IPs, databases with internet routes, missing flow logs.
Remediate one violation (move a workload, remove an IGW route) via IaC, not console.
Write the subnet policy as code (or doc): the shape, the rules, the audit cadence.

checks.hint: the shape is the security model

labs.title: Find the Waste
labs.objective: Run the classic waste queries and attribute every dollar to an owner.
steps: Unattached volumes, old snapshots, idle load balancers, oversized instances (CPU < 10% for 30d).
Total the monthly waste; attribute each item to a team via tags (or creator via CloudTrail).
Delete (or snapshot-then-delete) the safe items; file tickets for the ambiguous ones with owners.
Set up one recurring check (scheduled query + alert) for the biggest category.
Report: waste found, waste reclaimed, guardrail installed.

labs.title: Harden a Workload End to End
labs.objective: Take a sample app from default-insecure to hardened, verifying each layer.
steps: Deploy a sample app with default (insecure) settings: root user, writable filesystem, no probes.
Apply the hardened securityContext (non-root, read-only, drop ALL, seccomp); verify it runs.
Add a default-deny NetworkPolicy; open only the intended paths; verify.
Sign the image with cosign; configure admission to require the signature (or document the policy).
Attempt the break-in lab-style: try to write to the filesystem, escalate, and reach a denied peer — document what stopped you.

labs.title: Secrets Rotation Drill
labs.objective: Rotate a database credential with zero downtime using the ExternalSecrets pattern.
steps: Deploy ExternalSecrets (or simulate) syncing a DB password from a manager to a k8s Secret.
Configure the app to reload the secret without restart (file mount + reload, or restart with rolling update).
Rotate the password in the manager; watch the sync propagate; verify the app reconnects.
Verify the old password stops working (negative test) and audit logs show the rotation.
Document the rotation runbook: schedule, dual-credential window, rollback if the app fails to reconnect.

labs.title: GitOps from Scratch on kind
labs.objective: Install an agent, deploy from git, and watch self-heal correct drift.
steps: Install Argo CD or Flux on a kind cluster; connect it to a test git repo you control.
Create an Application syncing a simple app from the repo; verify it deploys and reports healthy.
Cause drift: kubectl edit the deployment (change replicas); watch the agent detect and revert it.
Promote: commit a tag bump via PR (simulate review); watch the agent sync the new version.
Document the loop: commit -> detect -> diff -> sync -> health. Time each stage.

labs.title: DR Drill: Wipe and Reconverge
labs.objective: Destroy the cluster and rebuild it from git alone, measuring the RTO.
steps: With the GitOps repo complete (apps + infra), delete the kind cluster entirely.
Recreate the cluster, reinstall the agent, point it at the same repos.
Time full convergence: all apps healthy, smoke tests passing.
Identify what did NOT recover (secrets? data?) — those are your DR gaps.
Write the DR runbook with the measured RTO and the gap list; schedule the next drill.

labs.title: Toil Audit and Elimination Plan
labs.objective: Measure your toil for two weeks, then write the elimination plan with ROI.
steps: Log every toil task for two weeks: manual deploys, tickets, hand-run queries, access grants.
Categorize and total hours; compute the toil ratio against team capacity.
For the top category, design the elimination: automate, self-serve, or remove the need.
Write the ROI: hours reclaimed per quarter vs build cost. Pitch it like a project.
Present to the team; commit to one elimination project with a date.

labs.title: Game Day: Zone Failure
labs.objective: Run a controlled zone-failure experiment with hypothesis and abort conditions.
steps: Write the experiment card: hypothesis ('lose AZ-b, traffic shifts <60s'), blast radius (staging), abort conditions (burn >5x, data loss signal).
Get explicit approval; announce the window; ensure rollback is one command.
Inject the failure (blackhole the AZ / cordon nodes); measure shift time, p99, errors.
Abort if conditions trigger; otherwise complete and record deviations from hypothesis.
File tickets for every deviation; schedule the verification re-run.

labs.title: Mock System Design, Recorded
labs.objective: Do a full 45-minute system design interview against the clock, recorded.
steps: Pick a prompt: design a CI/CD platform, a multi-tenant Kubernetes offering, or a secrets management service.
Set 45 minutes; follow the structure (clarify 10, sketch 15, deep-dive 13, trade-offs 7); narrate throughout.
Record (audio minimum); review for: time-boxing, questions asked, failure modes covered.
Identify the weakest segment; redo just that segment the next day.
Repeat weekly with a new prompt; track which segment improves.

labs.title: STAR Story Bank
labs.objective: Build and rehearse six STAR stories with numbers.
steps: Write six stories: outage mitigated, disagreement navigated, toil eliminated, mistake owned, platform shipped, incident learned-from.
Each: Situation (system + stakes), Task (your leverage), Action (what YOU did), Result (numbers).
Rehearse each aloud under 3 minutes; record and review for 'we' vs 'I' and missing numbers.
Get one peer review: which story is weakest? Rewrite it.
Keep the bank current: add a story per quarter.

simulations.title: The platform nobody uses
simulations.brief: The platform team shipped a beautiful IDP with 40 services. Adoption: 3 teams out of 25. The other 22 ship the old way — or with shadow tooling. Diagnose the adoption failure.

steps.symptom: IDP launched 8 months ago. Adoption: 3 of 25 teams. Shadow pipelines: 11 and counting.
evidence: Teams on platform: 3. Teams on legacy Jenkins: 11. Shadow tooling: 11.
'The golden path takes longer than our current way.' (19 teams)
options: The golden path isn't the easiest path — adoption comes from being easier than the alternative, not from mandates
Mandate the platform for all 25 teams immediately
The 22 teams are resistant to change — escalate to their managers
Build more platform features to attract users
steps.explain: An Internal Developer Platform is a product with developers as customers: golden paths are paved roads, not mandates. If the blessed way is slower than the old way, teams route around it — adoption comes from being the easiest path, period.

steps.symptom: The platform requires 14 form fields and 3 approvals to scaffold a service. The old way: one Jenkinsfile.
evidence: New service: 14 fields, 3 approvals, 2-5 day wait. Old way: copy Jenkinsfile, 10 minutes.
options: Reduce the scaffolding friction to beat the 10-minute alternative — every field and approval is a tax on adoption
The fields are necessary for governance — teams must adapt
Add a tutorial explaining why the fields matter
Hide the old Jenkins — remove the alternative
steps.explain: The platform competes with the status quo on every interaction: 14 fields and 3 approvals versus a 10-minute copy is a competition the platform loses. Each required field must justify itself against the adoption it costs.

steps.symptom: The 3 adopted teams love the platform — but they're the platform team's friends from a previous project.
evidence: Adopted: teams A, B, C — all previously worked with platform engineers.
Team D: 'We asked for help twice, got docs links. We stopped asking.'
options: Treat developer support as the product: office hours, pairing, and migration help — the platform team sells outcomes, not docs
The 3 teams prove the platform works — the rest will come
Docs links are sufficient support for senior engineers
Team D is a special case — ignore the outlier
steps.explain: Platform as product means developer support is the product: the teams that adopted had relationships, the ones that didn't got docs links. Office hours, pairing on migrations, and treating friction reports as bugs — that's the adoption engine.

simulations.debrief: Platform adoption is earned: the golden path must be the easiest path, scaffolding friction must beat the alternative, and developer support is the product. Mandates and features don't adopt platforms — outcomes do.

simulations.title: Template sprawl
simulations.brief: The software catalog lists 47 service templates. Half are unmaintained, 6 do the same thing, and new teams pick at random. Consolidate.

steps.symptom: 47 templates in the catalog. Maintained: 23. Duplicates: 6 web-service variants. Usage: scattered.
evidence: New team survey: 'We picked one at random. They all looked the same.'
options: Consolidate to a few parameterized templates with versioning and deprecation — each template is a maintenance liability
More templates means more choice — add the missing variants
Let teams maintain their own templates — decentralize
Delete templates at random until the number looks reasonable
steps.explain: Each template is a maintenance liability: 47 templates means 47 things to patch, secure, and update. Consolidate to a few parameterized templates with versioning and a deprecation path — choice without curation is just confusion.

steps.symptom: Consolidation proposed: 4 templates. Three teams protest — their variant has 'essential' differences.
evidence: Variant differences: port numbers, env var names, label conventions. No architectural differences.
'Our variant is essential because our deploy scripts expect port 8081.'
options: Parameterize the real differences (ports, names) and standardize the rest — essential means architectural, not habitual
Keep all variants — the teams know their needs
Force the 4 templates with no parameters — standardization above all
Let the protesting teams fork the platform
steps.explain: Parameterized templates absorb legitimate variation (ports, names, labels) while standardizing the architecture. 'Essential' differences that are just habits become parameters; the rest converges. Forking recreates the sprawl.

steps.symptom: 4 templates shipped with versioning. Now teams pin to v1 forever and never take updates.
evidence: Teams on template v1: 18. Current: v3. Security fixes in v2, v3: unapplied by 18 teams.
options: Publish a deprecation policy with timelines: old versions get security fixes for N months, then retire
Force-upgrade everyone to v3 overnight
Support v1 forever — stability is a feature
Security fixes aren't critical for templates
steps.explain: Templates need versioning and deprecation: without a sunset policy, every version lives forever and security fixes never land. A published timeline (security fixes for N months, then retire) makes upgrades a planned event, not a surprise.

simulations.debrief: Templates are products with lifecycles: consolidate to a few parameterized ones, version them, and deprecate on a published timeline. Unmaintained choice is worse than constrained choice.

simulations.title: The synchronous platform API
simulations.brief: The platform's provisioning API takes 90 seconds to create an environment — and times out half the calls. CI jobs hang, retries double-provision, and teams are building workarounds. Redesign the API contract.

steps.symptom: POST /environments takes 90s, times out at 60s in most clients. Retries create duplicate environments.
evidence: p50: 88s, p99: 140s. Client timeout: 60s. Duplicates from retries: 23 this month.
Handler: synchronous — provisions everything before responding. No idempotency key.
options: Make provisioning asynchronous: 202 Accepted with an operation ID, pollable status, idempotent retries
Increase all client timeouts to 180s
Make provisioning faster — 90s is the real problem
Tell teams not to retry
steps.explain: Platform APIs wrap slow operations asynchronously: 202 Accepted with an operation ID and pollable status, because the caller is usually automation. Idempotency keys make retries safe — the duplicate environments came from retrying a non-idempotent synchronous call.

steps.symptom: Async API shipped. Now failures surface as 'operation failed' with no detail — automation can't tell retryable from fatal.
evidence: Operation status: 'failed'. Reason: null. Retry policy: blind retry 3x.
Blind retries of fatal errors: 140 this month. Each provisions partial infra.
options: Return structured, actionable errors: machine-readable codes distinguishing retryable, fatal, and needs-input states
'Failed' is enough — humans can check the logs
Retry everything 10 times to be sure
Never fail operations — always return success
steps.explain: The caller is usually automation, so errors must be machine-actionable: structured codes for retryable vs fatal vs needs-input. 'Failed' with no reason forces blind retries — which is how partial infrastructure accumulates.

steps.symptom: The API is solid now, but every team wraps it differently — 9 client libraries, 4 of them broken.
evidence: 'Which client should we use?' — no canonical answer.
options: Ship and support one official client per ecosystem — the API contract includes its clients
Clients are the teams' problem — the API is documented
Ban custom clients
Deprecate the API — clients are too hard
steps.explain: A platform API's contract includes its clients: one official, supported client per ecosystem beats nine divergent wrappers. The API is the product — and products ship SDKs, not just docs.

simulations.debrief: Platform APIs are built for automation: async with operation IDs, idempotent, structured actionable errors, and official clients. The API is a product — design it like one.

simulations.title: Catalog with no owners
simulations.brief: The software catalog has 300 entries. 90 have no owner, 40 point at archived repos, and the 'runbook' links 404. The catalog is where services go to be forgotten. Fix it.

steps.symptom: 300 catalog entries. Owner missing: 90. Repo archived: 40. Runbook links dead: 61.
evidence: Entries: 300. owner: null on 90. repo archived: 40. runbook 404: 61.
Catalog lookups during incidents: 12% of incidents. 'We use Slack instead.'
options: Make ownership the minimum viable entry: no owner, no catalog entry — then enforce freshness with automation
More metadata fields will fix the catalog
Delete the catalog — Slack works fine
Hire someone to manually curate all 300 entries
steps.explain: The software catalog is the platform's front door, and ownership is the minimum viable entry: name, owner, lifecycle stage, repo and runbook links. A catalog that accepts ownerless entries becomes a write-only archive — enforce the minimum at write time.

steps.symptom: Ownership enforced for new entries. The 90 ownerless legacy entries remain — nobody claims them.
evidence: 90 ownerless entries. Claim campaign: 12 claimed, 78 silent.
3 of the 78 run in production. Nobody knows who deploys them.
options: Escalate the unclaimed production services: they get owners by deadline or they get sunset plans — unknown production ownership is a risk
Leave the 78 — they work fine without owners
Assign them all to the platform team
Delete all 78 immediately
steps.explain: Unowned production services are an operational risk with no accountable party. The campaign needs teeth: claim by deadline or the service gets a sunset plan. Assigning them all to the platform team just moves the fiction.

steps.symptom: Catalog is clean. Now entries rot again within months — repos move, owners leave, links die.
evidence: 6 months after cleanup: 34 entries stale again. Owner departures: 11.
Freshness process: quarterly manual review (never happened twice).
options: Automate freshness: sync from the repo, flag stale entries, and nudge owners — curation must be continuous, not quarterly
Do the manual review properly this time
Accept rot — catalogs are snapshots
Lock entries so they can't go stale
steps.explain: Catalogs rot because the world moves: owners leave, repos migrate. Manual quarterly reviews don't happen; automation does — sync ownership from the org chart, validate links continuously, and nudge owners when entries decay. Ownership first, rich metadata later, freshness always.

simulations.debrief: A catalog is a living system: ownership as the price of entry, teeth behind the cleanup, and automated freshness forever. The front door only works if someone maintains the building.

simulations.title: The escape hatch that became the road
simulations.brief: The golden path has an escape hatch for 'justified exceptions.' 60% of new services now use the hatch. The paved road is empty. Reclaim the golden path.

steps.symptom: Escape-hatch usage: 60% of new services. Golden path: 40%. The hatch was meant for rare exceptions.
evidence: New services: 60% escape hatch, 40% golden path. Hatch justifications: mostly blank.
'The golden path didn't support our database.' 'The hatch was faster.'
options: Treat hatch usage as product feedback: find out what the golden path lacks, fix it, and require real justification for the hatch
Remove the escape hatch — everyone on the golden path
The hatch is popular — make it the new golden path
Ignore it — 40% adoption is fine
steps.explain: Golden paths are paved roads, not mandates — but a 60% escape rate is the users voting with their feet. Each hatch use is feedback about what the paved road lacks; fix the road, and require genuine justification (reviewed, expiring) for the exceptions that remain.

steps.symptom: The top hatch reason: the golden path doesn't support the team's database. It never will — it's exotic.
evidence: Database: legacy proprietary, 2 services, no managed offering. Golden path: Postgres or MySQL.
Adding it to the golden path: 3 months of platform work for 2 services.
options: Keep it as a governed exception: documented, reviewed, expiring — not every snowflake belongs on the paved road
Add it to the golden path regardless of cost
Force the 2 services onto Postgres
Remove the database from the platform entirely
steps.explain: Escape hatches exist for justified exceptions — a legacy proprietary database for 2 services is exactly that. The answer is governed exception (documented, reviewed, expiring), not paving the road to every snowflake or forcing a migration that destroys value.

steps.symptom: Hatch usage is down to 8% with real justifications. Now platform leadership wants to report '100% golden path' by closing the hatch.
evidence: Hatch: 8%, all justified and expiring. Golden path: 92%.
'Can we get to 100% for the board slide?'
options: Keep the governed hatch: 100% is a vanity metric, and closing the hatch recreates shadow tooling
Close the hatch — 100% looks better
Report 100% and keep the hatch quietly
The 8% are failures — fix them
steps.explain: A governed 8% exception rate is the healthy steady state — it means the road serves 92% and the exceptions are visible and expiring. Chasing 100% for a slide recreates the shadow tooling the platform was built to replace. Report the honest number.

simulations.debrief: Golden paths need governed escape hatches: the hatch rate is product feedback, genuine exceptions get documented expiry, and 92% with honesty beats 100% with shadow tooling.

Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one

Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened

Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers

Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
